Thanksgiving Kale Slaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Thanksgiving Kale Slaw
Make a holiday-worthy slaw with shredded kale, cabbage, crispy fried shallots, and a shallot oil-infused maple Dijon vinaigrette.
Serves4 to 8
Makesabout 6 cups
Prep20 minutes
Cook15 minutes
Why You’ll Love Thanksgiving Kale Slaw
- This salad is one of my favorite things on the holiday table. It’s the perfect balance to all that heavy holiday food, and delicious enough to eat all season long.
- It’s make-ahead- and leftovers-friendly. All of the ingredients can be prepped (and even assembled) ahead of time so you can cross one time-sensitive dish off your list. Plus, the leftovers don’t get soggy!
- The shallots do triple duty. This little workhorse ingredient gives you a punchy raw bite, crispy fried shallots on top, and a deeply flavorful infused oil for the vinaigrette.
Nearly 10 years ago, I engineered a feat of unimaginable success: I made a genuinely crowd-pleasing Thanksgiving salad that can be made ahead of time (so I can stay out of my mom’s way) and actually keeps well as leftovers, provided there are any to box up at all. Today it’s still one of my favorite salads and things on the holiday table — the crunchy texture and bright flavor perfectly balance the richer dishes. That said, I developed it for a different time in my life and an entirely different circumstance.
When I made that salad, I was living in Houston and driving it over to my parents’ house as my contribution to dinner. Now I’m in Brooklyn and, more often than not, I’m the one hosting and making the whole freaking dinner in my little apartment kitchen. Suddenly, a little extra effort feels like a lot. So I thought maybe I could distill down the most important flavors of that salad and make something that still felt special, but perhaps a bit less fussy.
I kept the lacinato kale, but swapped shredded Brussels sprouts (a real time suck) for cabbage. Some chopped dates and roasted nuts give texture and little flavorful bits. The one non-negotiable: fried shallots. Frying shallots might be a little annoying, but it’s simple, can be done a day ahead, and truly makes the salad a star. In fact, I’m using shallots three ways: raw in the salad for some punch and crunch, fried to a shattering crisp, and then the infused oil is the base for a maple Dijon vinaigrette. The salad has everything I need to feel holiday-worthy without adding too much to my plate (pun intended).
Straight from Our Recipe Tester
“This is a unique and delicious slaw! Don’t skip the fried shallots. They add a wonderful crunch to the slaw. Plus using the shallot oil in the dressing adds a great depth of flavor to the kale/cabbage combo. I can’t wait to serve this up at the table this year.” —Kristina, November 2026
Why You Should Trust Me
I’m a professional recipe developer, but when I’m asked, people are often surprised to hear that my favorite food to eat, develop, and style for photos is salad — which is why I created my column, Salad Person. Whether I’m on my weekly (or more) farmers market crawl or meticulously surveying the grocery store produce, I’m constantly geeking out over seasonal fruits and vegetables. I love making salads that look gorgeous, taste even better, and will have your friends texting you for the recipe!
Key Ingredients in Thanksgiving Kale Slaw
- Kale: A base of lacinato (or Tuscan) kale will hold up to the dressing for days without losing the crunch factor.
- Cabbage: A little green cabbage breaks up all the kale, and retains its crunch even when dressed.
- Dates: Sweet, chewy dates add little pops of sweetness and textural variety.
- Shallots: Punchy raw shallots add a boost of sharp allium flavor, while crispy fried shallots make the perfect crunchy topping. Use the infused oil to boost the vinaigrette’s flavor.
Helpful Swaps
- Instead of olive oil, I love the buttery flavor of algae cooking oil.
- Swap out pecans or walnuts for roasted pistachios or almonds. Or, for a nut-free salad, try toasted pumpkin or sunflower seeds.
- Use dried cherries or Craisins instead of dates.
Salad Person is my column dedicated to making better, more delicious salads at home that you’re actually excited to eat. Each month, I’ll provide tips and techniques so you can enjoy them as much as I do — which is a lot!
Thanksgiving Kale Slaw Recipe
Make a holiday-worthy slaw with shredded kale, cabbage, crispy fried shallots, and a shallot oil-infused maple Dijon vinaigrette.
Prep time 20 minutes
Cook time 15 minutes
Makes about 6 cups
Serves 4 to 8
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
For the fried shallots and dressing:
- 1 cup olive oil
- 4 medium shallots, thinly sliced (1 1/2 cups)
- 3/4 teaspoon kosher salt, divided, plus more as needed
- 1/4 cup Champagne or white wine vinegar
- 1 clove garlic, finely grated or minced
- 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard
- 1 tablespoon maple syrup
- 1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, plus more as needed
For the slaw base:
- 1 medium bunch flat-leaf or lacinato kale (10 ounces total), stems removed and leaves thinly sliced crosswise into strips (3 1/2 to 4 packed cups)
- 2 cups finely shredded green cabbage (1/4 medium cabbage)
- 1 medium shallot, thinly sliced (1/2 cup)
- 1/3 cup fresh parsley or mint leaves, or a combination
- 1/2 cup roasted pecans or walnuts, coarsely chopped, divided
- 1/2 cup dried Medjool dates (5 to 6), pitted and coarsely chopped, divided
Instructions
Make the fried shallots and dressing:
- Line a plate with paper towels. Place 1 cup olive oil and 4 thinly sliced medium shallots in a medium skillet. Cook over medium heat, stirring frequently, until the shallots are golden-brown and crisp, about 15 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer the shallots to the plate and season with 1/4 teaspoon of the kosher salt.
- Transfer 1/3 cup of the shallot oil to a jar with a lid; reserve the remaining oil for another use. Add 1/4 cup Champagne vinegar, 1 finely grated garlic clove, 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard, 1 tablespoon maple syrup, the remaining 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt, and 1/4 teaspoon black pepper to the jar. Seal the jar and shake until combined. Taste and season with more kosher salt and black pepper as needed. (Alternatively, whisk the dressing together in a medium bowl.)
Assemble the slaw:
- Place 1 bunch thinly sliced flat-leaf kale leaves, 2 cups finely shredded green cabbage, 1 thinly sliced medium shallot, 1/2 cup fresh herb leaves, 1/4 cup of the coarsely chopped roasted pecans, 1/4 cup of the coarsely chopped dates, and half of the fried shallots in a large bowl. Add the dressing and toss to combine.
- Sprinkle with the remaining 1/4 cup coarsely chopped roasted pecans, 1/4 cup coarsely chopped dates, and fried shallots.
Recipe Notes
Make ahead
- You can fry the shallots up to 1 day ahead and store in an airtight container at room temperature. Refrigerate the oil.
- Prepare the dressing, kale, and cabbage up to 1 day ahead. Refrigerate the dressing and greens in separate airtight containers.
- The dressed slaw (without shallots) can sit at room temperature for up to 2 hours without wilting, making it a great make-ahead or buffet dish. Wait until just before serving to toss and top with the fried shallots so they stay crunchy.
Storage
- Leftover shallot oil can be refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 1 month.
- Leftover slaw can be refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 3 days.

I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
13:56:05 UTC
22:56:05 KST

Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud.
I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
After LG was accused of spying through its TVs, I wanted to see how other TV companies were collecting and protecting our data.
To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers.
Company representatives providing responses
Amazon: Eric Sveum, PR manager
Apple: Emily Ewing, public relations manager
Google: Alex García-Kummert, spokesperson
LG Electronics: Chris De Maria, director of public relations
Roku: Sarah Novatt, spokesperson
Samsung: Frank Giancamilli, corporate communications senior manager
TCL: Rob Manfredo, head of communications and events
One month ago, I invited 11 companies, including Amazon, Apple, Google, Hisense, LG, Panasonic, Roku, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Walmart’s Vizio to share those answers. We now have answers from the top three TV manufacturers as well as every major streaming device company. Some companies declined to answer. Below, you can see and compare how each company answered (or failed to answer) each question and then decide how you feel. (One company, Hisense, ignored our emails entirely.)
As you’ll see them say, some of this data collection is opt-in, and you can often opt out. We know that many TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) to figure out potentially everything we’re watching, and use that information to tailor ads, gather audience metrics, and serve up content recommendations based on our viewing habits. But though it sometimes seems like it’s required during the cavalcade of agreements thrown at us during setup, you can generally stop ACR even after you’ve agreed to it.
Opting out might not be as effective as it should be, however. A recent Northeastern University study found that Walmart’s Vizio kept on sending data after an opt-out (Vizio told me it was “routine operational data used to support the Vizio experience,” not ACR), while traffic with both Samsung and Roku was limited, but not stopped completely.
Below are the answers to our 17 questions. You will notice that some companies would not answer yes or no. We’ve also noted where companies declined to answer at all or ignored the questions. If any company becomes willing to directly answer our questions, we’ll add their responses.
1. Do your TVs ever use their embedded microphones, or the microphones in their remotes, to listen to sound in a customer’s home?
Amazon:
No. Fire TV includes voice functionality to help customers use their devices and get to content they love and fast, not to surveil homes. The microphones on our voice remotes are designed to only work when the mic button on the remote is physically pressed. And TVs with hands-free Alexa are designed to detect the wake word (and only the wake word) before connecting to Alexa. No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word. Customers can also turn off the microphones at any time. Every Fire TV smart television that has microphones also has a physical button or switch that disables the microphone.
Apple:
Apple TV 4K will use its far-field microphones and the Always On Processor strictly to listen for the Siri wake word. The Always On Processor does not process or act on any other sounds in the home. Users have full control over this and can turn off “Siri” or “Hey Siri” as a wake word, or disable Siri entirely. When using the Siri Remote, users must actively press and hold the microphone button for it to start listening.
Google:
If Google Assistant or Gemini is enabled or available, microphones (built-in hands-free ‘Hey Google’ or remote push-to-talk button) listen for activation triggers. Microphones remain in passive standby until triggered by hotword or button press.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.
LG:
Voice recognition is off by default and operates only if the user has opted in by accepting the Voice Information Agreement. Even if the user has opted in, they need to take additional steps for the microphone to be used. They must either press the microphone button on the remote control or they can use Hands-free Voice Control on supported models.
Hands-free Voice Control is disabled unless a user opts into this feature and then uses a wake-word. Wake-word detection is performed locally on the TV. If no wake word is detected, the audio is processed locally, promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.
Roku:
While Roku TVs don’t have built-in microphones, some Roku remotes do. Standard voice remotes listen only while the mic button is held, and hands-free remotes can be switched off.
Samsung:
No, for private monitoring. Samsung TVs do not listen to or record private conversations.
The TV’s embedded microphone only listens locally for the specific wake-up word (like “Hi, Bixby”) and ignores all other sounds, while the remote control microphone only activates when the customer physically presses the button.
Sony:
Sony did not provide an answer to this question.
TCL:
Some TCL TVs and remotes have microphones. Users can activate those microphones to use voice assistance features provided through third-party operating systems or applications. Those third parties control whether the voice features are available and how they are used, under their own terms and privacy policies.
Vizio:
Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.
2. Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?
Amazon:
No.
Apple:
Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.
Google:
[Recorded audio and/or transcripts based on audio are] stored only if ‘Voice & Audio Activity’ (VAA) is explicitly enabled under Google Account Web & App Activity. Voice & Audio Activity is off by default. If VAA is off, voice requests are processed in real-time and not saved to the Google Account.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.
LG:
If voice recognition is enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control’s microphone button or using the wake word), certain information generated as part of a specific voice recognition interaction may be stored locally on the TV to support voice-related features. Depending on the interaction, this may include Speech-to-text results derived from a user’s voice command.
Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, captured audio is promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.
Roku:
Voice commands made via voice-enabled remotes may be retained to improve voice features and provide support, consistent with Roku’s privacy policy. Users can opt out in their Roku account privacy settings.
Samsung:
No. Samsung Smart TVs do not store voice recordings or transcripts on the device.
However, on secure servers, voice commands and transcripts are stored only to process requests and improve voice assistant services.
Sony:
Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL does not collect audio data from TCL TV or remote microphones, or from the use of third-party voice features.
Vizio:

3. Do your TVs transmit any audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?
Amazon:
When customers speak to Alexa by pressing the mic button on the remote or using their chosen wake word, a recording of the request is sent to Amazon’s cloud, where a text transcript of the request is created to help Alexa provide a response. No audio is captured without the customer invoking Alexa—either by pressing the mic button or saying the wake word—and customers can easily review exactly what they asked and what Alexa heard, delete their recording, or even choose not to save them at all.
Apple:
Siri AI processes user requests using on-device processing, and when a request needs more powerful AI models, it extends those same on-device privacy protections to the cloud through a groundbreaking infrastructure called Private Cloud Compute (PCC). When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple, or anyone else, and outside experts can verify this privacy promise at any time.
For moments when users ask a question that requires up‑to‑date information, Siri AI can go out to the web and find it, then use Private Cloud Compute to generate an answer. Searches and requests are associated with a random identifier — a long string of letters and numbers — not a user’s Apple Account.
Google:
If Voice & Audio Activity is turned on, when voice features are activated (via hotword or remote button), captured audio or transcripts are transmitted to Google cloud servers for processing and fulfilling commands. If VAA is turned off, these are deleted.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.
LG:
Yes, but only if voice recognition has been enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control microphone button or using the wake word). When voice recognition is activated, the TV displays an on-screen indication that voice recognition is active and listening for the user’s command. Once the user finishes the voice command, the command is transmitted to our server, where it is converted into text and processed to respond to the command.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.
Roku:
Roku TVs don’t have microphones. Voice-enabled remotes let people control their Roku devices by voice, as described in our privacy policy.
Samsung:
No, for ambient or background listening. Samsung TVs do not passively monitor, record, or transmit audio from your home. Audio is only captured and transmitted when you actively initiate a voice command (such as pressing the microphone button on your remote or using the wake word). This voice input is processed securely to fulfill your requests, improve services, and support connected features under our voice privacy policies.
Sony:
Sony did not provide an answer to this question.
TCL:
TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.
Vizio:
Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

To operate ACR services, LG may process content-identification fingerprints together with device information, content source information, network information, and consent settings needed to support the feature. I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
13:56:05 UTC
22:56:05 KST

Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud.
I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
After LG was accused of spying through its TVs, I wanted to see how other TV companies were collecting and protecting our data.
To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers.
Company representatives providing responses
Amazon: Eric Sveum, PR manager
Apple: Emily Ewing, public relations manager
Google: Alex García-Kummert, spokesperson
LG Electronics: Chris De Maria, director of public relations
Roku: Sarah Novatt, spokesperson
Samsung: Frank Giancamilli, corporate communications senior manager
TCL: Rob Manfredo, head of communications and events
One month ago, I invited 11 companies, including Amazon, Apple, Google, Hisense, LG, Panasonic, Roku, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Walmart’s Vizio to share those answers. We now have answers from the top three TV manufacturers as well as every major streaming device company. Some companies declined to answer. Below, you can see and compare how each company answered (or failed to answer) each question and then decide how you feel. (One company, Hisense, ignored our emails entirely.)
As you’ll see them say, some of this data collection is opt-in, and you can often opt out. We know that many TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) to figure out potentially everything we’re watching, and use that information to tailor ads, gather audience metrics, and serve up content recommendations based on our viewing habits. But though it sometimes seems like it’s required during the cavalcade of agreements thrown at us during setup, you can generally stop ACR even after you’ve agreed to it.
Opting out might not be as effective as it should be, however. A recent Northeastern University study found that Walmart’s Vizio kept on sending data after an opt-out (Vizio told me it was “routine operational data used to support the Vizio experience,” not ACR), while traffic with both Samsung and Roku was limited, but not stopped completely.
Below are the answers to our 17 questions. You will notice that some companies would not answer yes or no. We’ve also noted where companies declined to answer at all or ignored the questions. If any company becomes willing to directly answer our questions, we’ll add their responses.
1. Do your TVs ever use their embedded microphones, or the microphones in their remotes, to listen to sound in a customer’s home?
Amazon:
No. Fire TV includes voice functionality to help customers use their devices and get to content they love and fast, not to surveil homes. The microphones on our voice remotes are designed to only work when the mic button on the remote is physically pressed. And TVs with hands-free Alexa are designed to detect the wake word (and only the wake word) before connecting to Alexa. No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word. Customers can also turn off the microphones at any time. Every Fire TV smart television that has microphones also has a physical button or switch that disables the microphone.
Apple:
Apple TV 4K will use its far-field microphones and the Always On Processor strictly to listen for the Siri wake word. The Always On Processor does not process or act on any other sounds in the home. Users have full control over this and can turn off “Siri” or “Hey Siri” as a wake word, or disable Siri entirely. When using the Siri Remote, users must actively press and hold the microphone button for it to start listening.
Google:
If Google Assistant or Gemini is enabled or available, microphones (built-in hands-free ‘Hey Google’ or remote push-to-talk button) listen for activation triggers. Microphones remain in passive standby until triggered by hotword or button press.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.
LG:
Voice recognition is off by default and operates only if the user has opted in by accepting the Voice Information Agreement. Even if the user has opted in, they need to take additional steps for the microphone to be used. They must either press the microphone button on the remote control or they can use Hands-free Voice Control on supported models.
Hands-free Voice Control is disabled unless a user opts into this feature and then uses a wake-word. Wake-word detection is performed locally on the TV. If no wake word is detected, the audio is processed locally, promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.
Roku:
While Roku TVs don’t have built-in microphones, some Roku remotes do. Standard voice remotes listen only while the mic button is held, and hands-free remotes can be switched off.
Samsung:
No, for private monitoring. Samsung TVs do not listen to or record private conversations.
The TV’s embedded microphone only listens locally for the specific wake-up word (like “Hi, Bixby”) and ignores all other sounds, while the remote control microphone only activates when the customer physically presses the button.
Sony:
Sony did not provide an answer to this question.
TCL:
Some TCL TVs and remotes have microphones. Users can activate those microphones to use voice assistance features provided through third-party operating systems or applications. Those third parties control whether the voice features are available and how they are used, under their own terms and privacy policies.
Vizio:
Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, captured audio is promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.

3. Do your TVs transmit any audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?
Amazon:
When customers speak to Alexa by pressing the mic button on the remote or using their chosen wake word, a recording of the request is sent to Amazon’s cloud, where a text transcript of the request is created to help Alexa provide a response. No audio is captured without the customer invoking Alexa—either by pressing the mic button or saying the wake word—and customers can easily review exactly what they asked and what Alexa heard, delete their recording, or even choose not to save them at all.
Apple:
Siri AI processes user requests using on-device processing, and when a request needs more powerful AI models, it extends those same on-device privacy protections to the cloud through a groundbreaking infrastructure called Private Cloud Compute (PCC). When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple, or anyone else, and outside experts can verify this privacy promise at any time.
For moments when users ask a question that requires up‑to‑date information, Siri AI can go out to the web and find it, then use Private Cloud Compute to generate an answer. Searches and requests are associated with a random identifier — a long string of letters and numbers — not a user’s Apple Account.
Google:
If Voice & Audio Activity is turned on, when voice features are activated (via hotword or remote button), captured audio or transcripts are transmitted to Google cloud servers for processing and fulfilling commands. If VAA is turned off, these are deleted.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

Once the user finishes the voice command, the command is transmitted to our server, where it is converted into text and processed to respond to the command.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

{
	"0xdeadf1sh/AssemblyForNeovim",
	config = function()
		require("asm").setup()
	end,

- <leader>a in normal mode: function under the cursor

Attention to Mamba: A Recipe for Cross-Architecture Distillation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
13:29:46 UTC
22:29:46 KST

Attention to Mamba: A Recipe for Cross-Architecture Distillation
AuthorsAbhinav Moudgil†**, Ningyuan Huang‡**, Eeshan Gunesh Dhekane, Pau Rodríguez Lopez, Luca Zappella, Federico Danieli
State Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba have become a popular alternative to Transformer models, due to their reduced memory consumption and higher throughput at generation compared to their Attention-based counterparts. On the other hand, the community has built up a considerable body of knowledge on how to train Transformers, and many pretrained Transformer models are readily available. To facilitate the adoption of SSMs while leveraging existing pretrained Transformers, we aim to identify an effective recipe to distill an Attention-based model into a Mamba-like architecture. In prior work on cross-architecture distillation, however, it has been shown that a naïve distillation procedure from Transformers to Mamba fails to preserve the original teacher performance, a limitation often overcome with hybrid solutions combining Attention and SSM blocks. The key argument from our work is that, by equipping Mamba with a principled initialization, we can recover an overall better recipe for cross-architectural distillation. To this end, we propose a principled two-stage approach: first, we distill knowledge from a traditional Transformer into a linearized version of Attention, using an adaptation of the kernel trick. Then, we distill the linearized version into an adapted Mamba model that does not use any Attention block. Overall, the distilled Mamba model retains most of the original Pythia-1B Transformer performance, reaching a perplexity of 14.01 close to the teacher’s 13.86. This largely carries over to downstream tasks, although some gaps appear on tasks relying more on in-context recall. To show the efficacy of our recipe, we conduct thorough ablations at 1B scale with 10B tokens varying sequence mixer architecture, scaling analysis on model sizes and total distillation tokens, and a sensitivity analysis on tokens allocation between stages.

Mamba introduces input selectivity to its SSM layer (S6) and incorporates convolution and gating into its block definition. EventSourcingDB 1.3.0 Is Available
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
13:19:45 UTC
22:19:45 KST

EventSourcingDB 1.3.0 is Available
EventSourcingDB 1.3.0 is out, and it is faster and more stable than any version before it. Writing and EventQL queries are considerably faster, reading is faster as well, every request is bounded in time, and more than sixty fixes went in. Next to all that, it brings a new API that reports the outcome of every request it accepts in its body and names every error with a code of its own.
This post walks through what changed and what to mind when you upgrade. The v1 API is supported until January 31, 2027, and a later release removes it, so you can move to the new one at your own pace. And from today on, the documentation of EventSourcingDB lives on eventfoundation.io; every old link leads there.
A New API, Built to Last#
The new v2 API runs next to the v1 API, on the same data. Its central idea is simple: once the server has accepted a request, its outcome is in the body. A request counts as accepted when it is authenticated, its body has the shape its route expects, and it stays within its limits. A precondition that does not hold, an event type that is not known, a database in read-only mode – all of these come back as an answer the client can read, rather than as a status code it has to interpret.
Every error carries a code that is a link to its own page, which explains why it happens and how to fix it. You will find them all under Errors. Streamed answers that come to an end, such as reading events, close with an explicit end item, so a client can tell a complete answer from one that was cut off. While a stream waits, the server sends heartbeats through it, which keeps a proxy from closing it in between.
The v2 API also brings recursive preconditions: isSubjectPristine, isSubjectPopulated, and isSubjectOnEventId can now apply to a subject together with every subject below it. That is useful whenever a decision depends on a whole part of the tree rather than a single subject.
The current versions of all eight client SDKs speak both APIs and use the v2 API wherever the server offers it. So apart from updating your SDK, you do not have to change your code, as long as a proxy in front of the database lets through the HTTP method QUERY, which the v2 API uses for reading. If you call the HTTP API directly, Migrating to v2 shows what changes, route by route.
Moving and Backing Up Data#
Exporting and importing make it easier to move events into a new database. Both work with one plain CloudEvent per line, including its ID and time, so an export imports without any conversion. Since the import computes the hashes itself, you can also export a history, remove personal data from it, and import the result without having to compute any hash by hand.
Incremental backups hold only the events written since a previous backup. A restore takes a full backup followed by its increments, which keeps regular backups of a large database small. Restoring itself has become considerably faster too, since it now writes events in batches.
Faster, and Sturdier Under Load#
Writing is considerably faster, for one client as for many at once, and it no longer slows down as the store grows. Running EventQL queries is considerably faster as well, most of all for queries that read many events, group, sort, or join several sources, and so is reading events. The indexes take far fewer files, so reading the events of a subject gets faster in large databases, and verifying the integrity of the store reports every inconsistency it finds, up to a hundred, rather than only the first.
Much of the other work in 1.3 is invisible until you need it. Every request, every answer, and every idle connection is bounded in time, so a slow or stuck client can no longer hold resources forever. EventQL queries have limits on how deeply they nest and how much memory they hold, which keeps a single query from overflowing the stack or taking as much memory as it likes.
The server compares the API token in constant time and refuses to start with one that could be guessed. And if it fails to store a write, for example because the disk is full, it switches to read-only mode until it is restarted, keeps serving reads, reports this through its health endpoint, and names the cause in its log. Limits lists the bounds.
Running in Production#
A few additions are aimed at running EventSourcingDB in production. Rate limiting is enabled by default and scales with the size of the machine, so a single client that sends far too many requests cannot overwhelm the database. The health endpoint of the v2 API speaks OpenMetrics, which means you can scrape it with Prometheus and similar tools directly, and it reports more about the process, such as its memory and its file descriptors; Logging and Monitoring lists what it reports.
If you want to make sure that only known event types are ever written, the new flag --require-event-schemas rejects writes and restores of events whose type has no registered schema. It is off by default. And an API catalog at /.well-known/api-catalog points tools to the OpenAPI documents of both APIs.
Before You Upgrade#
This release asks for some care when upgrading. Please read Upgrading EventSourcingDB before you start; these are the points that matter most:
- Back up your data first. A data directory that 1.3 has opened cannot be opened by an earlier version again, so a backup is the only way back.
- Stop the old server before you start 1.3. Versions up to 1.2 do not lock the data directory, so a rollout that starts the new server first, such as a Kubernetes Deployment with RollingUpdate, would run two servers on the same data, which can damage it.
- The Docker image runs as another user, UID 65532 instead of 100. A data directory that an earlier image wrote has to be handed over to the new user once, or the container keeps running as the old one; the guide shows both, for Docker and for Kubernetes.
- The API token needs at least 32 characters, unless the server runs with a temporary data directory, and it has to be printable ASCII without whitespace at its start or end. Otherwise, the server refuses to start.
- Update your client SDKs first if your applications verify event hashes, since 1.3 writes a new version of the event hash, and older SDKs report every event written after the upgrade as tampered with.
- The flags --ai-model and --ai-option are gone, since EventAI leaves the management UI; a server that is still started with them no longer starts.
- Check your EventQL queries and preconditions: 1.3 changes, among other things, how values of different types compare, treats the ID of an event as a string, and takes dates and times in UTC, which can change their results or make them fail.
- The first start rebuilds the indexes: 1.3 starts right away and serves reads and writes, but refuses EventQL queries and a few other requests until it is done, which can take several minutes.
The upgrade guide and the changelog list everything else that needs attention, such as stricter rules for the source of events and for event schemas.
Time to Upgrade, or to Start#
Faster where it counts, sturdier where things go wrong, and with a new API next to the one you know: that is 1.3. If you are already running EventSourcingDB, the upgrade guide gets you there safely.
And if you have not tried EventSourcingDB, the database built for Event Sourcing, this is a good moment to start. Installing EventSourcingDB gets you the binaries and the Docker image, and the Quickstart takes you from starting the server to writing and reading a first event in a few minutes. We'd love to hear what you build with it.

After testing the unit, Alicia noted that her reheated meals tasted significantly better than if they had been microwaved, adding that its lightweight build makes it perfect for transit commuting. It's a total win-win!
Say goodbye to the inconvenience of renting bulky carpet cleaning equipment — this compact yet effective upholstery cleaner handles it all. A popular pick on TikTok, it harnesses the power of steam to lift stubborn stains from rugs, carpets, kitchen chairs, and more. With its dual spray and suction mechanism, you can count on removing spots permanently.

Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
12:56:24 UTC
21:56:24 KST

Some of the most impressive tech that Adobe showcases at its annual Max conference each year is the experimental features it’s developing, and the latest of those tools are being announced today: they can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process.
Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters
Here are some of the experimental ‘sneaks’ being showcased at Adobe Max.
The first (and weirdest, in my opinion) is Project Screen Test, which is designed to make AI-generated characters easier to develop and use for video content. Instead of just describing how the character should sound and behave in text prompts, the tool lets you talk to the character and direct them in an audition-like environment. You start by describing some base personality traits, such as “anxious, shy, awkward,” and giving the character a voice, either by selecting a preset, describing how it sounds in a prompt, or uploading sample audio for it to reference.
You can then expand its persona in further detail by conversing with the character as if you’re talking on FaceTime, outlining its backstory, temperament, goals, flaws, fears, movement quirks and more. Once you’re happy, the tool lets you generate animated screen tests with the character by describing an environment or scenario you want to put them in.
This is currently a standalone creative exercise, and it’s not clear how (or if) it could feature in any of Adobe’s existing AI video tools. The results provided a more identifiable and consistent personality compared to many soulless animated AI characters I’ve seen, but that’s the entire reason this exists — AI video generation provides far less creative control compared to traditional animation, where every aspect of a character is included with absolute intention.
There’s also Project Sight Span, which reframes photographs and images by turning them into a 3D environment that you can navigate through and reposition. The 3D space generates objects and backgrounds that are outside of the original frame, but feel like a natural part of the image, even if you’re turning to see what’s behind you. While the visuals in the 3D environment are pixelated and ill–defined, the resolution quality is restored when you select your chosen angle.
Sight Span works with any flat image, including photos, paintings, and illustrations, and can preserve and replicate artistic styles. Even repositioned tattoos and facial features in photographs remain surprisingly recognizable and true to the original reference. It’s a bit like a version of Apple’s Spatial Reframing feature on steroids: you can reposition more aggressively and change the shooting point entirely if you want, but it also feels far less deserving of being called a photo afterward.
Project Sound Bender is an AI audio mixing feature that lets you customize sound effects as if you’re clicking your cursor around a color wheel. It works by uploading a video clip and then describing your desired audio in a text prompt, such as “bubbling sci-fi cauldron noises.” Sound Bender then generates sound effects and automatically syncs it to the video, and provides a square sound canvas that lets you adjust the noises in real time. Each corner of the canvas will automatically assign a relevant AI-generated sound, such as dense gurgling with popping bubbles, rumbling boiling rocks, pitched bloops, and crackling electric fire. You can drag your cursor around the canvas to select which noises stand out the most, or customize each corner with different sound effects.
Adobe also showcased Project Rinse Repeat, which lets you copy edits and then automatically apply them to other objects or people in the same photo. For example, if you painstakingly airbrush out acne or blemishes on one person, Rinse Repeat will adapt your specific changes to anyone else in a group of people who need similar touchups. It can also be used to add shadows to products in marketing graphics, even if the objects are different shapes and sizes. Rinse Repeat is built around Photoshop, and the edits you apply to other subjects remain fully editable because the tool recreates them with native Photoshop tools.
These “sneaks” are tech previews of capabilities that might eventually be developed into tools for Adobe’s Creative Cloud apps or Firefly platform, so there’s no guarantee that they’ll graduate into being available features. Almost all of these projects are built around Adobe’s generative AI developments, however, and given AI tools now play a central role in the company’s growth strategy, it’s likely that at least some of the experiments will see an official launch. As wacky or fun as these AI experiments are, they’re also an omen. If they’re useful enough, that means AI may eventually replace the tools and stock libraries that creative professionals currently use, regardless of how complex their feelings are about the technology.
A notable theme across these sneaks is making complicated photo editing, filmmaking, and audio mixing workflows feel more accessible and intuitive, adapting them into something that’s more interactive and easy to use. In some cases the features almost seem like toys, but with the benefit of allowing you to make practical changes to creative projects.
“Making these interactions more intuitive is also about giving experienced creatives more precise control,” senior principle Adobe research scientist Gautham Mysore, told The Verge. “Sound Bender’s sonic exploration capability and Sight Span’s camera positioning are examples of how professionals could apply their judgment and refine a result more directly. That connection between creative intent and control is a big part of what we’re exploring.”

Open research, stronger privacy: Making Firefox users harder to fingerprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
12:44:06 UTC
21:44:06 KST

Firefox is strengthening protection against trackers that recognize you across websites, even when they don’t use cookies. The latest fingerprinting protections shipped in Firefox reduce the extractable distinguishing details, making more Firefox users look alike to tracking scripts and strengthening individuals’ privacy in everyday browsing.
These protections build on our research into browser and device fingerprinting, a technique that combines details about your browser and device to identify you across websites. We investigated which details contribute most to make users uniquely identifiable, turned those findings into practical protections for Firefox users, and shared our results openly so the wider web security and privacy community can build stronger defenses.
Our findings are documented in the research paper Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild, which has been accepted for publication at Computer and Communications Security (CCS) 2026, a leading international conference on computer security and privacy. We’ve also created an easier-to-digest website and browser test suite to help explore the findings in the paper.
Cookie-less Tracking
Browser fingerprinting combines details about your browser and device, such as available fonts, screen dimensions, and graphics hardware, to build a uniquely recognizable profile. Each piece may seem ordinary, but together, they can enable trackers to single you out across websites, even without storing a cookie.
Effective fingerprinting protection starts with understanding which browser details trackers rely on most. Our research found that protecting just a handful of browser features can significantly weaken popular fingerprinting techniques. That finding enabled us to focus on Firefox’s protections where they can make the biggest difference and bring those benefits to all Firefox users.
To evaluate these techniques, we simulated the browser measurements collected by fingerprinting scripts from Fingerprint Pro, Signifyd, and Akamai and examined how their combinations distinguish users. The study used measurements collected from nearly 25 million Firefox users, with additional privacy safeguards beyond Mozilla’s existing data collection policies.
Those safeguards included OHTTP, which routed encrypted requests through a relay. The relay sees the user’s IP address but not the request contents, while Mozilla receives the contents without the user’s IP address. We also tightly limited data access and retention: individual telemetry records were deleted several months ago and only aggregate results were retained and published for open science. Our research paper explains the method, safeguards and ethical considerations in detail.
Less distinctive, more private
Our approach reduces unnecessary differences in the information Firefox exposes to websites. For example, Firefox limits the information exposed through screen resolution APIs to hide the size and position of the system taskbar or dock, preventing that desktop layout detail from contributing to a fingerprint. As another example, it can report processor counts as either 4 or 8 instead of exposing the exact count, which can make a browser more distinctive.
Our goal is to make more users’ browsers look similar to fingerprinting scripts while preserving the information websites need to function correctly, like language and timezone settings. Firefox also uses randomization to make other fingerprinting signals less useful to trackers, though the benefits of these techniques are harder to quantify and fall outside the measurements reported here.
In our evaluation, these protections (the most recent of which shipped in Firefox 145) substantially degraded the precision of fingerprinting in Firefox both by reducing the number of users with unique fingerprints and increasing the size of the groups of users that share a fingerprint.
The research also enabled us to identify why certain measurements differed between users. Addressing these differences produced more consistent outputs for image rendering, Web Audio, and mathematical operations on Android, reducing the distinguishing details available to fingerprinters.
These results show that substantial reductions in browser fingerprint uniqueness are achievable and provide meaningful progress toward stronger online privacy. These do not make fingerprinting impossible as trackers can surely adapt. But our research provides a concrete, measurable improvement in browser defenses against online tracking.
The built-in privacy protections in Firefox are complemented with capabilities and options to further strengthen the protection against online fingerprinters. Built-in and always-on Total Cookie Protection in Firefox segments stateful identifiers and prevents trackers from following you across your browsing using cookies. Firefox Relay provides you with unique email masks, preventing websites from linking your subscriptions to other sites via data brokers. And Firefox now integrates a free VPN that masks your IP address to protect against tracking and fingerprinting. Together with Firefox’s enhanced fingerprinting protections, these capabilities provide everyone a very strong foundation to take back control of their privacy online.
Research that improves everyday browsing
Privacy protections need to work on the websites people use every day. These findings allow us to prioritize changes that deliver measurable privacy benefits while keeping those websites working.
Some of Firefox’s fingerprinting protections, such as hiding the size of your taskbar or dock, are on by default in all browsing modes. Others are introduced first in Private Browsing and Strict Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) mode, while we work toward enabling them by default, following the same strategy we’ve used for years. To enable these additional protections in all your Firefox windows, select Strict in the Enhanced Tracking Protection settings. Follow the steps here if the “Strict” protections get in the way of any website functionality.
Want to explore browser fingerprinting yourself? Visit the research project page to try the fingerprinting test and learn more about our findings. For a closer look at what we measured and how we turned those insights into Firefox protections, explore our paper: Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild.
We’ll keep strengthening Firefox’s privacy protections while continuing to work in the open. By sharing our research, our code, and what we learn, we’re shaping the web we envision: free, private, secure, and accessible to all.

Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
12:30:17 UTC
21:30:17 KST

Last week, MIT CSAIL published Sparks of Weight-Space Programming. Given the raw weights of a small network, GPT-6 Astra could tell which game it had been trained to play. Given only a game’s rules, it could write the weights of a small network from scratch and beat networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. No gradients, no training loop, just reasoning about what the weights compute. They coined this weight-space programming.
In another experiment, they asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math by editing its weights. Astra changed only 0.016% of the weights, and MATH-500 accuracy jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%.1
Looking at Astra’s edit, I realized most of its search was solving a linear program by trial and error. It spent about 8 hours and 28 forward passes choosing which weights to change and by how much. A couple of LP solves, about a minute each, do the same job with 8× fewer changed weights. In this post I’ll walk through the edit, why it’s an LP, and what that says about the fix itself.
Thinking loops#
Small reasoning models have a common failure: they get stuck in thinking loops, repeating the same few lines over and over instead of finishing their reasoning. Qwen3.5-0.8B is especially prone to it, and its model card says so. On MATH-500, 93% of the base model’s answers ran into the 32,768-token limit without ever reaching an answer.
The edit fixes the loops, so it helps anywhere the model loops. That includes instruction following: IFEval went from 21% to 62%.
On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, Astra couldn’t meaningfully improve its math ability. As the authors put it, editing the weights could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but couldn’t add one the model lacked.
How Astra fixed the loops#
Transformers use residual connections: each layer’s output is added to its input rather than replacing it. Follow one token through the network and you get a single vector that every layer adds to, called the residual stream (1,024-dimensional in this model). When the model is looping, the residual stream shifts in a consistent direction. Astra’s fix was to edit two layers so that what they add points the opposite way.
Finding the loop direction#
Astra wrote four pairs of short texts, each a piece of productive reasoning and a looping version of the same reasoning. It ran all eight through the model and recorded each token’s residual stream vector at one layer. Averaging over the looping texts gives one vector, and averaging over the productive texts gives another. Their difference, normalized, is the loop direction $u$: the way the residual stream moves when the model loops.
Editing the weights#
Each MLP ends with a matrix $W$ (called down_proj). At every token, it turns the MLP’s 3,584-dimensional hidden activation $h$ into a 1,024-dimensional output $Wh$, which gets added to the residual stream $x$:
So the MLP’s output is always a weighted sum of the same 3,584 vectors, the columns $w_j$ of $W$. $W$ fixes what those vectors are; the activations $h_j$ decide how much of each one gets added at each token.
Each column points partly along $u$. That amount, $u^\top w_j$, is how much column $j$ pushes the model toward looping whenever $h_j$ is active. Astra’s edit subtracts a multiple $\alpha$ of it:
$$w_j \to w_j - \alpha \, (u^\top w_j) \, u$$
At $\alpha = 1$ the component along $u$ is gone, so the column no longer pushes toward looping. Doing this to every column in layers 15 and 19 took accuracy from 9% to 33% on GSM8K and MATH training problems. At $\alpha = 6$ the component is flipped: a column that wrote $+a$ along $u$ now writes $-5a$, and pushes the model away from looping whenever it’s used.
Every edited column changes by a multiple of the same vector $u$. So the whole edit is one direction $u$ plus one number per column, $v_j = -\alpha\,(u^\top w_j)$, which is zero for columns left alone. That’s a rank-1 change:
$$\Delta W = u\,v^\top$$
At each token, it adds $(v \cdot h_t)\,u$ to the residual stream: some amount of $u$, set by how active the edited columns are. No other direction changes.
That leaves $v$ to choose: which columns to edit, and how large $\alpha$ should be. Astra worked it out by trial and error, testing each edit on a fresh batch of those training problems:
Pushing harder than $\alpha = 1$ helped more, and a random direction did nothing. The final edit used $\alpha = 6$ on only the 64 columns per layer that wrote the most $u$ on looping text.
Where the time went#
The paper released Astra’s full logs: every tool call, every forward pass, every note it wrote to itself. Astra had a Python kernel with the weights loaded and a budget of 50 forward passes, each a batched run of the model on training problems or texts of its choosing.
The edit was frozen after about 10 hours, and the last 17 passes re-tested it without changing anything.2 Of those 10 hours, finding $u$ took 15 minutes. Finding $v$ took about 8 hours.
Choosing v is a linear program#
Astra was searching for a $v$ that strongly pushes looping tokens away from $u$ while barely touching productive ones. Since the push at token $t$ is $v \cdot h_t$, linear in $v$, both requirements are linear inequalities.
I labeled tokens from the base model’s own traces: looping tokens ($R$), deep inside a loop, and productive tokens ($P$), well before any loop starts,3 and recorded their activations $h_t$ at layers 15 and 19. Each one becomes a constraint, and the LP picks the $v$ with the smallest L1 norm $\sum_j |v_j|$:
$$ \begin{aligned} \min_v \quad & \sum_j |v_j| \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & v \cdot h_t \le -\delta && t \in R \quad \text{(at least } \delta \text{ away from } u\text{)} \\ & |v \cdot h_t| \le \varepsilon && t \in P \quad \text{(at most } \varepsilon\text{)} \end{aligned} $$
In practice no $v$ satisfies every constraint, so each one gets a penalized slack variable.
Minimizing L1 tends to make $v$ sparse. The L1 ball is a diamond, and when you grow it until it touches the feasible region, it usually touches at a corner, where most coordinates are exactly zero. So the LP picks the columns as well as the amounts.
To get exactly 8 columns per layer, I kept the 8 with the largest effect and solved again with the rest fixed at zero.4
That replaces Astra’s 8-hour search, including its choice of columns and $\alpha$, with a couple of LP solves. An off-the-shelf solver (HiGHS) took over 20 minutes each on these constraints, so I wrote a GPU solver (PDHG, the algorithm behind PDLP) that gets within 0.2% of its optimum in about a minute.5
Results#
I tested two LP edits. Both use Astra’s layers. One uses Astra’s direction $u$. The other uses a heuristic direction: label tokens in the model’s own traces as looping or productive with a simple repetition detector, then take the difference of their average residual streams. It’s the same recipe Astra used, minus the hand-written texts, so no LLM is involved. I tuned the LP’s settings on a separate 128-problem dev set; everything in the chart and table is on data never used for fitting or tuning.
With Astra’s direction, the LP matches Astra’s edit on every benchmark, within noise, while changing 8× fewer weights. With the heuristic direction, it gets about 93% of the way there.
A few other things showed up:
- The search mattered, and the LP replaces it. On the dev set, reusing Astra’s recipe (top 64 columns, $\alpha = 6$) on the heuristic direction without searching again scores 44.5. The LP scores 54.7.
- Different columns, same fix. The LP’s 8 columns share only 3 (layer 15) and 1 (layer 19) with Astra’s 64. Many sparse solutions work; what matters is the total push along $u.$
- A random direction does nothing. On the dev set, a random $u$ of the same size scores 10.2, against 10.9 for the base model.
A steering vector does the same job#
An edit can only tell a looping token apart from a productive one through its activations, and a loop isn’t recognizable from them until it’s well under way.6 So on the dev set, asking the LP to push only on loop-like tokens did no better than pushing on every token.
The LP’s 8 columns in layer 15 are active on 89% of tokens, and the push they add barely varies from token to token, so the edit is close to a constant push along $u$. A constant push doesn’t need a weight edit. It can be added directly as a steering vector, a fixed vector added to the residual stream at every token.
The table below adds the LP edit’s average push along $u$ to the unedited model at layers 15 and 19, at three strengths:
For comparison, on the same runs: the LP edit scores 62.5 on the dev set and 53.2 on MATH-500, Astra’s edit 59.4 and 50.0, the base model 10.9 and 7.0. MATH-500 here is one sample per problem.
At 1×, the steering vector recovers essentially the whole fix. The window is narrow: at 0.5× the loops come back, and at 2× they stop but the reasoning falls apart.
The only difference is delivery. The LP edit is an ordinary checkpoint; the steering vector needs extra code at inference time.
Limitations and what’s next#
This is one model. The LP still relies on Astra for the layers, and the best results use Astra’s direction too. The heuristic direction gets most of the way without an LLM, but not all of it.
Loops also turned out to be fixable with a constant push, so the LP’s per-token constraints didn’t end up mattering much. A behavior that should change some tokens and leave others alone would be a better test of them. Choosing the layers without an agent is the other open piece.
Lastly, this was only tested on removing loops. Many other behaviors, like refusal or sycophancy, can be steered by adding or removing a single direction in the residual stream.7 If a behavior can be steered with one direction, choosing how to build it into the weights should be the same LP, but that still needs testing.
Code, edits, and the full write-up are on GitHub.
Citation#
Please cite this work as:

- Astra’s full run took 158 turns and 20.3 hours, 4.7 of them an outage. 19 forward passes failed and weren’t counted against its budget. The full breakdown is in the write-up. ↩︎
- A token counts as repeated if the 16 tokens ending at it already appeared earlier in the answer. A loop starts at the first point after which at least 80% of the remaining tokens are repeats. Looping tokens are repeats at least 64 tokens into a loop. Productive tokens come at least 256 tokens before it, or anywhere in an answer that finished. ↩︎
- Each column is ranked by $|v_j|$ times the standard deviation of $h_j$, roughly how much it adds along $u$ at a typical token. ↩︎
- PDHG (primal-dual hybrid gradient) only needs matrix-vector products, so all the token constraints fit on the GPU at once, and it returns an exactly sparse $v$. ↩︎

So the MLP’s output is always a weighted sum of the same 3,584 vectors, the columns $w_j$ of $W$. $W$ fixes what those vectors are; the activations $h_j$ decide how much of each one gets added at each token.
Each column points partly along $u$. That amount, $u^\top w_j$, is how much column $j$ pushes the model toward looping whenever $h_j$ is active. Astra’s edit subtracts a multiple $\alpha$ of it:
$$w_j \to w_j - \alpha \, (u^\top w_j) \, u$$
At $\alpha = 1$ the component along $u$ is gone, so the column no longer pushes toward looping. Doing this to every column in layers 15 and 19 took accuracy from 9% to 33% on GSM8K and MATH training problems. At $\alpha = 6$ the component is flipped: a column that wrote $+a$ along $u$ now writes $-5a$, and pushes the model away from looping whenever it’s used.
Every edited column changes by a multiple of the same vector $u$. So the whole edit is one direction $u$ plus one number per column, $v_j = -\alpha\,(u^\top w_j)$, which is zero for columns left alone. That’s a rank-1 change:
$$\Delta W = u\,v^\top$$
At each token, it adds $(v \cdot h_t)\,u$ to the residual stream: some amount of $u$, set by how active the edited columns are. No other direction changes.
That leaves $v$ to choose: which columns to edit, and how large $\alpha$ should be. Astra worked it out by trial and error, testing each edit on a fresh batch of those training problems:
Pushing harder than $\alpha = 1$ helped more, and a random direction did nothing. The final edit used $\alpha = 6$ on only the 64 columns per layer that wrote the most $u$ on looping text.
Where the time went#
The paper released Astra’s full logs: every tool call, every forward pass, every note it wrote to itself. Astra had a Python kernel with the weights loaded and a budget of 50 forward passes, each a batched run of the model on training problems or texts of its choosing.
The edit was frozen after about 10 hours, and the last 17 passes re-tested it without changing anything.2 Of those 10 hours, finding $u$ took 15 minutes. Finding $v$ took about 8 hours.
Choosing v is a linear program#
Astra was searching for a $v$ that strongly pushes looping tokens away from $u$ while barely touching productive ones. Since the push at token $t$ is $v \cdot h_t$, linear in $v$, both requirements are linear inequalities.
I labeled tokens from the base model’s own traces: looping tokens ($R$), deep inside a loop, and productive tokens ($P$), well before any loop starts,3 and recorded their activations $h_t$ at layers 15 and 19. Each one becomes a constraint, and the LP picks the $v$ with the smallest L1 norm $\sum_j |v_j|$:
$$ \begin{aligned} \min_v \quad & \sum_j |v_j| \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & v \cdot h_t \le -\delta && t \in R \quad \text{(at least } \delta \text{ away from } u\text{)} \\ & |v \cdot h_t| \le \varepsilon && t \in P \quad \text{(at most } \varepsilon\text{)} \end{aligned} $$
In practice no $v$ satisfies every constraint, so each one gets a penalized slack variable.
Minimizing L1 tends to make $v$ sparse. The L1 ball is a diamond, and when you grow it until it touches the feasible region, it usually touches at a corner, where most coordinates are exactly zero. So the LP picks the columns as well as the amounts.
To get exactly 8 columns per layer, I kept the 8 with the largest effect and solved again with the rest fixed at zero.4
That replaces Astra’s 8-hour search, including its choice of columns and $\alpha$, with a couple of LP solves. An off-the-shelf solver (HiGHS) took over 20 minutes each on these constraints, so I wrote a GPU solver (PDHG, the algorithm behind PDLP) that gets within 0.2% of its optimum in about a minute.5
Results#
I tested two LP edits. Both use Astra’s layers. One uses Astra’s direction $u$. The other uses a heuristic direction: label tokens in the model’s own traces as looping or productive with a simple repetition detector, then take the difference of their average residual streams. It’s the same recipe Astra used, minus the hand-written texts, so no LLM is involved. I tuned the LP’s settings on a separate 128-problem dev set; everything in the chart and table is on data never used for fitting or tuning.
With Astra’s direction, the LP matches Astra’s edit on every benchmark, within noise, while changing 8× fewer weights. With the heuristic direction, it gets about 93% of the way there.
A few other things showed up:
- The search mattered, and the LP replaces it. On the dev set, reusing Astra’s recipe (top 64 columns, $\alpha = 6$) on the heuristic direction without searching again scores 44.5. The LP scores 54.7.
- Different columns, same fix. The LP’s 8 columns share only 3 (layer 15) and 1 (layer 19) with Astra’s 64. Many sparse solutions work; what matters is the total push along $u.$
- A random direction does nothing. On the dev set, a random $u$ of the same size scores 10.2, against 10.9 for the base model.
A steering vector does the same job#
An edit can only tell a looping token apart from a productive one through its activations, and a loop isn’t recognizable from them until it’s well under way.6 So on the dev set, asking the LP to push only on loop-like tokens did no better than pushing on every token.
The LP’s 8 columns in layer 15 are active on 89% of tokens, and the push they add barely varies from token to token, so the edit is close to a constant push along $u$. A constant push doesn’t need a weight edit. It can be added directly as a steering vector, a fixed vector added to the residual stream at every token.
The table below adds the LP edit’s average push along $u$ to the unedited model at layers 15 and 19, at three strengths:
For comparison, on the same runs: the LP edit scores 62.5 on the dev set and 53.2 on MATH-500, Astra’s edit 59.4 and 50.0, the base model 10.9 and 7.0. MATH-500 here is one sample per problem.
At 1×, the steering vector recovers essentially the whole fix. The window is narrow: at 0.5× the loops come back, and at 2× they stop but the reasoning falls apart.
The only difference is delivery. The LP edit is an ordinary checkpoint; the steering vector needs extra code at inference time.
Limitations and what’s next#
This is one model. The LP still relies on Astra for the layers, and the best results use Astra’s direction too. The heuristic direction gets most of the way without an LLM, but not all of it.
Loops also turned out to be fixable with a constant push, so the LP’s per-token constraints didn’t end up mattering much. A behavior that should change some tokens and leave others alone would be a better test of them. Choosing the layers without an agent is the other open piece.
Lastly, this was only tested on removing loops. Many other behaviors, like refusal or sycophancy, can be steered by adding or removing a single direction in the residual stream.7 If a behavior can be steered with one direction, choosing how to build it into the weights should be the same LP, but that still needs testing.
Code, edits, and the full write-up are on GitHub.

We need more goat sacrifices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
12:29:48 UTC
21:29:48 KST

Just a quick thing before this week’s post. If you’ve preordered THE STRANGEST IDEA IN THE WORLD, I’d like to send you a little something extra in the mail. Submit your preorder receipt and your mailing address here. This is only available to folks with US or UK addresses—apologies to those who live elsewhere! In the US, everyone with a valid entry will get one; in the UK they’ll pick winners randomly. The link will be open until December 11, and we’ll start mailing things out after that.
