- Models see time used against a 10-, 30-, or 45-minute limit. Setup doesn’t count; thinking and game calls do. Models can’t end an episode early.
- Run limits
- Game execution stops after roughly 1 second without state changes, 5 seconds without output, or 60 seconds overall, and returns diagnostics.
Why test 100,000 inputs? The game checks a small set of cases per run. Our headline count requires a fresh-game replay and 100,000 passing tests on the independent TIS-100-CXX simulator, providing stronger evidence that a program generalizes to new inputs.
One record up close
Undecimal Twin RounderSPEC44149538, one of the eight tournament puzzles, rounds an input to the nearest multiple of N on one output and of 11−N on the other. When we froze the leaderboard, the best community program took 2,694 cycles. Opus 5.5 passed its first program after 6.5 minutes, at 5,669 cycles. It went under the record 16 minutes in and finished at 1,918, which is 29% faster. That speed cost one more node and 28 more instructions than the old record.
The core of the program is a two-speed search. Instead of subtracting N one step at a time, nodes 5 and 6 subtract 4N until they overshoot, then add N back until the value turns positive. Each drives a small coprocessor, node 2 or node 7, by sending it jump offsets through a port, so the coprocessor works as a lookup table for 4N and N.
Loading puzzle trajectories…
Five models got under the old record in-game. The other two cycle records are GPT-6.1 Sol’s 3,460 on Intersection IdentifierSPEC64160260, against 3,872 (11% faster), and Gemini 4 Argon’s 188 on Error: 8SPEC79324720, against 198 (5% faster). All three are on tournament puzzles, none in the main game. Of the 133 new frontier points, 18 beat a community record outright. The other 115 are new tradeoffs: better balances between the three scores than any community solution.
What separates the models
Cost doesn’t track quality
GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 75.6 record proximity at an estimated $0.75 per puzzle. Opus 5.5 reaches 77.2 at $5.08, 7 times the cost for 2 more points. Fable 5.1 is the most expensive at $7.19 and scores 70.2.
Activity doesn’t explain quality either. GPT-6.1 Sol averages 136 game calls per puzzle at 75.6 record proximity; Gemini 4 Argon averages 41 at 76.2.
New points concentrate on hard puzzles
New frontier points appear on 14 hard puzzles, 4 medium puzzles, and no easy ones. Long-running puzzles are harder to solve but easier to improve: on puzzles with a cycle record of 200 or less, 88% of episodes pass and 4% find a new point. Above 500 cycles, 76% pass and 8% find one.
Speed is the hardest score
Every model is closest to the community on nodes and furthest on cycles. Across all 13, mean proximity is 72 for nodes, 56 for instructions, and 45 for cycles.
What the models built
We grouped all 55 puzzles by their main demand, then read the programs. Fifteen of the sixteen models solved all five routing puzzles, and none found a new frontier point there. The examples below show how different designs spend the same resources.
Multiplication: spend code to save cycles
Signal Multiplier43786 has no MUL. Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Astra use JRO, a relative jump, to enter a block of repeated instructions at the right position. The jump selects how many copies of a value to send and add, saving the counter updates and branches of a multiplication loop.
Gemini 4 Argon’s fastest program uses two paths to multiply in parallel and a final node to interleave their outputs. It takes 436 cycles against GPT-6 Astra’s 523, about 17% faster, at a cost of two more nodes and 33 more instructions.
Window sums: distribute the history
Signal Window Filter60099 outputs the sums of the last three and last five inputs, so a solution has to remember history as well as add. Gemini 4 Argon’s four-node program uses SWP to rotate stored values and ADD/SUB to update running state. GPT-6.1 Sol spreads that delay and aggregation across seven nodes, passing intermediate values between them.
GPT-6.1 Sol’s program runs in 318 cycles with 26 instructions; Gemini 4 Argon’s takes 428 cycles with only 17. The difference is how much of the work runs in parallel, and how much communication and code that costs.
Indexed access from stacks
T31 Node EmulatorNEXUS.23.727.9 needs eight addressable storage slots, but the available memory nodes are stacks. These programs move values between stacks to reach the requested slot, then read or replace it. MiMo-V2.6-Pro uses counted transfer loops; Opus 5.5 uses JRO to pick among unrolled transfers, spending extra instructions to save cycles.
Memory isn’t one skill: MiMo-V2.6-Pro solves this emulator but fails Sequence Mode CalculatorNEXUS.09.904.9 and Signal Window Filter60099.
Each row is that model’s fastest saved program for the puzzle, picked for illustration. Not all are new frontier points.
God mode: what if the model could see the target?
The main benchmark hides the community’s scores. In a separate study on six puzzles, five models got:
- The target: exact community scores, showing which tradeoffs remain unbeaten.
- Diagnostics: cycle-by-cycle traces and profiles of where each node stalls.
- Edge cases: a fast simulator that runs 10,000 random tests and returns failures.
- More time: 30 minutes, plus extensions for progress, up to 60.
Every model improved: GPT-6 Astra from 82.8 to 91.8, GPT-6.1 Sol from 82.9 to 90.6, Opus 5.5 from 81.4 to 89.1, Grok 4.7 from 67.5 to 75.1, and Gemini 4 Argon from 83.5 to 87.9 in mean record proximity. Scores rose in 28 of the 30 model–puzzle pairs.
The diagnostics changed what models did next. On Signal Multiplexer22280, GPT-6.1 Sol’s first passing program took 294 cycles. Its profile showed node 2 working 86% of the time while nodes 1 and 3 spent 84% blocked waiting to write to it. GPT-6.1 Sol moved the branching out of node 2 and into those two neighbors. The next run took 204 cycles, 31% faster, at a cost of two more nodes and five more instructions.
Information, tools, and time all changed together, so this study can’t say which addition helped most. These runs are outside the main leaderboard and the headline count.
Puzzles: Signal Multiplexer, Sequence Generator, Signal Edge Detector, Interrupt Handler, Sequence Peak Detector, and Signal Error Corrector.
Co-discovery
We submitted selected programs to the leaderboard, and the community improved on them almost immediately. On Undecimal Twin RounderSPEC44149538, @LongingForRest took Opus 5.5’s 1,918-cycle program and cut it to 1,744 by the next day. The record is now credited to both: LongingForRest/opus-5-5.
Neither got there alone. The models found new tradeoffs quickly, and players read those programs, worked out why they worked, and took them further.
Mathematics is seeing the same shift. Terence Tao and colleagues used LLM-guided search across 67 problems and improved on the best known results in several. In “After Math,” Silvia De Toffoli and Eamon Duede argue that a result only becomes a solution once mathematicians can understand it, and that AI fits better as an assistant than a competitor. TIS-100 is a small, measurable version of that future: a model finds a better program, and people turn it into something they understand.
Pareto explorer
Choose a puzzle and model, then select a point to see its scores and the program that produced it. Every puzzle also has its own page with records and the best programs: all 55 puzzles.
The plot shows cycles and instructions; node counts can differ. New frontier points are judged on all three scores.
Download all 3,714 model Pareto points (CSV) · all 3,714 programs (ZIP), also on GitHub and Hugging Face. 186 rows are marked as new frontier points, which pool to 133 across models.
Methods
Expand
Suite. All 22 campaign puzzles, all 25 TIS-NET puzzles, and eight tournament puzzles from 2018: 19 easy (10 minutes), 17 medium (30), and 19 hard (45). Every model has one scored episode per puzzle. Time limits differ by difficulty, so difficulty and search time can’t be separated.
Scoring. Each model–puzzle pair contributes one selected attempt, with no best-of-attempts scoring, so solve rates are pass@1: a puzzle counts as solved when that one episode saved a program that replays in a fresh game. Unsolved puzzles stay in every average and score zero.
New frontier points. The reference is the community leaderboard as of October 15, 2026. Ties don’t count. Models found 154 candidate points on 23 puzzles. Our count pools and deduplicates them across models and keeps the 133 on 18 puzzles with fresh-game replay and 100,000 passing tests. Testing is strong evidence of correctness, not proof.
Record proximity. The community record divided by the model’s best score, averaged across the three scores and all puzzles, ×100. Each score can come from a different program.
Limits. One episode per pair compares the configurations as tested and doesn’t measure repeated-run variability. Spread between puzzles is variation across tasks. Public puzzles may overlap with training data. Mechanic groups are our own labels.
Programs. Every model Pareto point’s program is public under the MIT License, in TIS-100 save format and named like the community leaderboard’s files (<puzzle>.<cycles>-<nodes>-<instructions>.txt). They are mirrored as one file per program on GitHub and as a table on Hugging Face. Two points replay in the game but fail some random tests; they are included and never count as new frontier points.
Resources. Costs are estimated from recorded October 2026 API list prices, including cache discounts. Tokens accumulate across responses, so repeated input counts again, and tokenizers differ. Game calls count individual dispatched tools, including errors, and exclude the automatic final submission.

Microsoft is now rolling out Automatic Super Resolution (Auto SR), an upscaling technology that competes with Nvidia’s DLSS, for the Xbox Ally X, Xbox Ally X20, and select Windows Copilot Plus PCs, the company announced today. Auto SR is also getting some new features alongside this official release.
Microsoft’s DLSS competitor is out for the Xbox Ally X and works in handheld mode
With the official launch of Auto SR, your Xbox Ally X can use Microsoft’s upscaling technology undocked and with games running at 1080p.
In April, Microsoft started testing Auto SR on the Xbox Ally X, but you could only use it while docked. The full release of Auto SR announced today now works while you’re playing handheld and running on battery, and it also supports games running at 1080p. Microsoft does note that playing in handheld and at 1080p might lead to performance that “may not be as optimal as other configurations,” but says you’ll see visual improvements “especially in older games.”
Previously, Auto SR was also limited to framerates of “around” 60 to 75fps, but support for a new Auto SR Performance mode will allow you to hit framerates of up to 120fps. The Performance mode, and new compatibility with Auto HDR, will be available through Windows updates.

====================================================================================================

AI is an information gateway. Audiences still don't want it making their news
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
00:15:33 UTC
09:15:33 KST

In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”
As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.
For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,” we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.
The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.
Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.
Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.
Conversational AI as a friction-reducing information intermediary
Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more quickly.
“Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.
We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).
Using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.
Many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.
At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.
As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.
Persistent attitudes: People’s views on generative AI in journalism and news
As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.
People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.
This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.
Zooming out
Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.
First, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.
Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also shows that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.
Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.
The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.
Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily users and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.
This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.
Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

Sony’s latest Pulse wireless headset packs planar magnetic drivers at a good price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
23:43:37 UTC
08:43:37 KST

It’s tempting to seek out the do-everything wireless gaming headset with noise cancellation, phenomenal sound quality, multiplatform connectivity, swappable batteries — you name it. But if you just want the basics done well, Sony’s new $99.99 PlayStation Pulse headset is worth considering. It has very good sound and just enough extras, even if you use more gadgets than just your PlayStation 5.
Sony’s latest Pulse wireless headset packs planar magnetic drivers at a good price
A comfortable, minimalist option that supports concurrent low-latency audio and Bluetooth.
Inside the Pulse’s nondescript ear cup shells are custom planar magnetic drivers, which deliver clean, detailed sound whether you’re gaming, listening to music, or both. They aren’t bass-heavy or too shrill; their default equalizer is pleasing and punchy, though you can also tweak it in the PS5’s interface, like other Pulse headsets. They’re not Sony’s first audio gaming product to feature this type of high-end driver (the first was in 2023), but they are the most affordable at $99.
The Pulse comes with either a white or black headband, with a soft-touch underside and a decent amount of give near the top of your head where it rests its weight. Thankfully, the headset is lightweight and offers size adjustments that go beyond what my large head requires for comfort. These are some of the only headphones I’ve used with ear cups that can rotate 180 degrees in either direction.
Functionally, the Pulse stands out as a semi-affordable wireless headset that can stream audio from PlayStation Link (Sony’s low-latency, lossless wireless connection) and Bluetooth simultaneously. It includes a USB-C Link dongle that lets you pair it quickly with whatever you plug it into, whether it’s a PS5, PC, or Nintendo Switch 2.
The headset’s ear cup controls include a dedicated Bluetooth button that, beyond pairing with another gadget, lets you pause or resume Bluetooth content (it can also answer or hang up calls). You can also control Bluetooth audio volume using the integrated volume rocker, but only when a device isn’t connected via PlayStation Link. In simultaneous audio mode, the rocker adjusts audio solely for the device connected via the Link dongle.
If you have Sony’s PlayStation Portal, the Pulse can connect directly to the handheld without the Link dongle, just as Sony’s Pulse Elite and Explore can. It’s so convenient, and I hope Sony pushes for more devices that integrate the Link wireless technology in the future.
The Pulse isn’t the only headset that Sony has in the works. Its Pulse Edge wireless headset doesn’t have an exact launch date or price, but the company touts that it packs in twice as many magnets in its drivers (eight versus four), active noise cancellation, and a detachable boom mic that will likely provide better-sounding voice audio than the built-in mic in the standard Pulse. It will also include game / chat audio controls, a 3.5mm jack, and a carrying case.
While the $99 Pulse is comparatively light on features, Sony’s focus on providing standout audio quality and comfort makes it worth seeking out if you have a PS5 and are on a strict budget for your next wireless headset.

The DRAM interface and the PHY (why a DDR3+ interface must be tuned at boot)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
23:41:41 UTC
08:41:41 KST

This chapter explains what happens on the wires between the FPGA and the DRAM, and why a DRAM interface must be tuned at boot. It covers the signals, the strobes, the board topology, the leveling procedures, the termination and the reference voltages, then the clocks of the FPGA and the DFI interface between the controller and the PHY.
Each section ends with the part of LiteDRAM that implements the mechanism. The previous chapter, DRAM in a nutshell, explained the commands and the timings; Initialization and calibration gives the exact steps the BIOS runs.
A DRAM interface has two halves. The command and address half goes one way, from the controller to the DRAM, and is shared by every chip of a rank. The data half is bidirectional and split into byte lanes, each with its own strobe. The figure below shows the signals.
A byte lane is 8 DQ, their DQS pair and their DM. Each lane is routed on its own, so each one can arrive at a slightly different time, and each one is tuned on its own.
In LiteDRAM, the pads of the DRAM are a record from the platform file, with fields named after
these signals (dq, dqs_p, a, ba, cs_n). The PHY counts the lanes from it. Two helpers
of litedram/common.py reshape the pads: PHYPadsReducer keeps some lanes only, and
PHYPadsCombiner merges chips with separate command buses into one controller.
SDR memory transfers one word per clock, sampled on the rising edge of the clock that the controller sends. DDR memories transfer two words per clock, one on each edge, and at these rates the clock from the controller cannot be trusted to sample the data: the delays of the board and of the chips are too large.
The data therefore travel with their own clock, the strobe DQS: the side that sends the data also sends DQS, and the receiver samples DQ with it. This is a source-synchronous interface. Both travel the same path, so their delays cancel. The figure below shows how DQS is aligned with DQ.
On writes the controller sends DQS centre aligned, its edges in the middle of each bit. On reads the DRAM sends DQS edge aligned, on the bit transitions, and the receiver delays it by a quarter of a clock. Before the burst, DQS is driven for a preamble, and after it for a postamble, without carrying data.
In LiteDRAM, the DDR PHYs shift the write DQS by a quarter of a clock from DQ, with the means of its FPGA:
- The Artix-7 PHY clocks its DQS serializers from a clock shifted by 90 degrees, sys4x_dqs,
which the target builds (bench/arty.py).
- The PHYs with output delays (Kintex-7 and Virtex-7 HP banks, UltraScale) delay DQS by a quarter of a clock.
- The Lattice and Gowin PHYs take the shifted write clock of the DQS block of their FPGA.
On reads, the PHYs differ:
- The Xilinx PHYs do not use DQS. They sample DQ with their own fast clock, through an input delay that read leveling tunes per lane.
- The Lattice and Gowin PHYs use the DQS blocks of their FPGA, which delay DQS by 90 degrees, capture DQ with it and report when they saw a burst (burst detect).
DDR3 and DDR4 route the clock, command and address pins as one bus that passes by every chip in turn and ends on a termination: the fly-by topology. It keeps these heavily loaded signals clean at high rates, but each chip receives the clock a little later than the previous one. The figure below shows it.
The data lanes are point to point, so their delays do not follow the clock. A chip needs DQS to arrive close to its own CK edge (tDQSS). With fly-by routing the skew between the first and the last chip can exceed a clock period, so each lane needs its own DQS delay.
Write leveling measures that delay. The controller sets the DRAM into write leveling mode with a mode register bit (MR1 bit A7 on DDR3 and DDR4), then sends DQS pulses. The DRAM samples its CK with each DQS rising edge and returns the sampled value on DQ. The controller delays DQS step by step until DQ goes from 0 to 1: DQS is then aligned with CK at that chip.
In LiteDRAM, the PHYs expose write leveling through registers: wlevel_en enables the mode,
wlevel_strobe sends one DQS pulse, and per-lane output delays move DQS and DQ. The BIOS runs the
scan (sdram_write_leveling in liblitedram).
Write leveling needs output delays: the Kintex-7 and Virtex-7 PHYs in HP banks and the UltraScale
PHYs have them. The Artix-7 has none: with one static DQS phase, only some lanes of a fly-by
memory meet tDQSS. Its optional CK phase shift mode (with_ck_phase_shift, DDR3 at 1:4) moves CK
against all the lanes instead (CK phase shift).
Write leveling aligns DQS with CK within one clock period, but a lane can be one whole clock early or late: the DRAM then writes the burst shifted by a few words. Write latency calibration writes a known pattern, reads it back, and moves each lane by whole clocks until the pattern is right.
DQ-DQS training then centres DQ against DQS on writes. It sweeps the output delay of the DQ pins of each lane, writes and reads back a pattern at each step, and keeps the middle of the passing range. It relies on a working read side, which read leveling then refines.
In LiteDRAM, the write latency is moved by write bitslips (wdly_dq_bitslip) and DQ by output
delays (wdly_dq). Each PHY declares which calibrations it supports in its settings
(write_leveling, write_latency_calibration, write_dq_dqs_training, read_leveling); the
BIOS runs only those.
On reads, the controller does not know when the data arrive. The DRAM answers CL clocks after RD, but the board and the I/Os add a delay that differs per lane. Two settings must be found for each lane: a coarse one, which fast clock cycle holds the first word, and a fine one, where in the bit to sample.
The coarse setting is a bitslip: the deserializer output is shifted by whole bits until the words line up. The fine setting is an input delay, from a few picoseconds to about a hundred per step depending on the FPGA (78 ps on 7-Series with a 200 MHz reference). Read leveling writes a pattern, then for each bitslip sweeps the delay and reads the pattern back. The figure below shows such a scan.
The window is the data eye seen through the delay line. A wide window means a robust interface; a narrow one points to a signal integrity or clocking problem. DDR3 and DDR4 can also return a fixed pattern from their MPR (multi-purpose register), so the read side can be tuned before anything has been written.
The PHYs that capture with DQS have one more problem: DQS is not driven between bursts, so the receiver must listen to it only during a read. The FPGA's DQS block opens this gate and reports a burst detect, which read leveling uses to confirm that the read window is right.
In LiteDRAM, each PHY declares its number of delay taps and bitslips in its settings (delays,
bitslips), and exposes them through registers (rdly_dq_inc, rdly_dq_bitslip, and
burstdet_seen on the Lattice and Gowin PHYs). The BIOS runs the scan and prints one line per
lane and bitslip. On DDR4 it reads the MPR patterns, except on registered DIMMs and clamshell
layouts.
At DRAM rates, a signal reflects at the end of a line that is not terminated. The DRAM therefore terminates its own data pins with an on-die termination (ODT): a resistor switched on when the ODT pin is high. The FPGA terminates its inputs in the same way when it receives read data.
DDR3 and DDR4 have two termination values: RTT_NOM, used when the chip is idle or another rank is written, and RTT_WR, used while the chip itself is written (dynamic ODT). The driver strength of the DRAM, RON, sets how hard it drives the read data. All three are set in the mode registers.
In LiteDRAM, the defaults of the table are set by litedram/init.py; a PHY can override them
(rtt_nom, rtt_wr, ron in its settings). With the DRAM DLL off, a DDR3 mode for low
clock rates that the GW5A PHY offers (dll_off), both terminations are disabled.
The ODT pin is driven statically by default. With with_dynamic_odt (DDR3, single rank), the
controller raises ODT only around writes, so the DRAM terminations are off during reads
(Dynamic ODT). The FPGA side termination is part of the I/O standards of the
platform file, not of LiteDRAM.
The resistance of the drivers and terminations of a chip varies with the process, the voltage and the temperature. DDR3 and later chips calibrate them against a precision resistor on their ZQ pin, 240 ohm to ground. ZQCL, the long calibration, runs once at initialization; ZQCS, the short one, corrects the drift from time to time during operation.
In LiteDRAM, the initialization sequence ends with ZQCL (Mode registers and power-up), and the refresher sends ZQCS once per second by default (Refresh). LPDDR4 has no ZQCS: it calibrates with two multi-purpose commands (MPC), start and latch, which LiteDRAM sends at initialization only.
The data receivers compare each input to a reference voltage, VREF, set halfway between the high and the low levels. On DDR3 the board provides VREF on dedicated pins. DDR4 terminates its data pins to the supply (pseudo open drain), so the data swing sits near the top of the supply and the right reference is not halfway. The DRAM generates its data VREF internally, programmed in MR6.
On the FPGA side, the receivers of the read data also need a VREF. Some FPGA I/O banks can set it internally, in steps, instead of using a VREF pin.
In LiteDRAM, the DDR4 initialization writes MR6 with tCCD_L only and leaves its VREF field at zero, the first value of range 1 (60% of VDDQ): the DRAM data VREF is not trained.
The UltraScale+ PHY can set the FPGA read VREF of its HP I/O banks (with_hpio_vref, register
rd_vref, codes 0 to 72). The BIOS does not scan it: the register keeps its build-time value
(hpio_vref_tune) unless software writes it. LiteX issue 2769 tracks the missing BIOS sweep.
An FPGA fabric cannot run at the DRAM clock: a DDR3 at 800 MT/s has a 400 MHz clock and moves data at 800 Mbps per pin. The PHY therefore uses the serializers and deserializers of the FPGA I/Os. The controller runs at a fraction of the DRAM clock, and moves several clocks' worth of commands and data per cycle.
This fraction is the frequency ratio. At 1:4, the controller runs at a quarter of the DRAM clock: the Arty A7 bench target runs its controller at 125 MHz, its DRAM clock at 500 MHz, and its DDR3 at 1000 MT/s. For a DDR memory, the data rate is twice the DRAM clock: at 1:4, eight times the controller clock.
An Artix-7 DDR3 target needs four clocks, generated by a PLL in the board's clock module
(bench/arty.py). The Kintex-7 and Virtex-7 targets need no sys4x_dqs: their output delays shift
DQS instead.
Other families use their own clocking: the ECP5 PHY uses a 2x clock for its I/O gearing and a 4x clock at 1:4, and the Gowin GW5A PHY selects 1:2 or 1:4 with its number of phases. DDR PHYs gives the clocks of each family.
The controller and the PHY meet at a DFI interface, named after the DDR PHY Interface specification. It carries, for each DRAM clock of a controller cycle, one command slot and the data of that clock. Each of these slots is a DFI phase. The figure below shows the phases at a 1:4 ratio.
Two latencies tie the commands to their data. The write latency is the number of controller cycles between WR and the cycle where the controller presents the write data. The read latency is the number of cycles between RD and the cycle where the read data come back valid. Both follow from CL, CWL and the pipeline of the PHY.
The commands do not always start on phase 0. The PHY tells the controller on which phase to issue
reads and writes (rdphase, wrphase), so that the data of a burst fill whole controller cycles.
In LiteDRAM, the DFI interface is Interface of litedram/phy/dfi.py. It follows the structure of
the DFI specification, phases and signal names, without claiming a version of it.
Each PHY fills a PhySettings with its number of phases, its latencies in controller cycles, CL and CWL in DRAM
clocks, and its calibration capabilities. DFIRateConverter wraps a PHY to raise the ratio, with
more phases and narrower data per phase. See Core architecture.
Each PHY is built from the I/O primitives of its FPGA family. The table below summarizes what the LiteDRAM PHYs use; DDR PHYs describes each one.
The 7-Series input and output delays need a reference clock of 200 or 300 MHz, or 400 MHz on the
faster speed grades; their output delays exist only in the HP banks of Kintex-7 and Virtex-7. The UltraScale delays are set in time
units, and the FPGA compensates them for voltage and temperature while en_vtc is set.
Where to go next: Initialization and calibration for the BIOS steps, DDR PHYs for each family, Debugging when a scan shows no window.

Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Notion AI Chats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Notion AI Chats 19
			
		 	
				Fireworks AI says its October breach was broader than initially disclosed, with attackers gaining access to customer account and billing information as well as some datasets, incomplete model weights and secrets. Notion, the popular productivity and note-taking app, disclosed that it was impacted in the breach but "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces" were involved. "Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results." The Hacker News reports:  In a notice published on October 10, 2026, [Fireworks AI] said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT. [...] The latest bulletin from the company reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously thought. The company said attackers reached its development environment via an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development (R&D) machines on October 23, 2026.
"On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," it added. "As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use." The breach is said to have provided access to the following types of information: [Resource metadata; Billing information; and Model weights and datasets]. Fireworks AI said payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not impacted by the security incident. It also said it's alerting customers whose data was impacted.

Serve Robotics wants to democratize sidewalk delivery robots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
22:53:03 UTC
07:53:03 KST

Serve Robotics is opening up its platform to make its autonomous last-mile delivery robots available to anyone who wants to use them. The company is launching a new AV Delivery Developer Portal, enabling third-party software engineers, independent businesses, and even autonomous AI agents to access its fleet of 2,000 sidewalk robots.
Serve Robotics wants to democratize sidewalk delivery robots
With its new developer platform, the sidewalk robot company lets small businesses, indie developers, and AI agents summon its 2,000-robot fleet without paying delivery app markups.
With this new capability, third-party developers and interested small businesses can use Serve’s software tools to dispatch robots directly without relying on major food delivery companies, like Uber Eats. Now, anyone who lives in one of the 150 neighborhoods where the company currently operates can employ a sidewalk robot for deliveries.
Serve, which was spun out of the app-based delivery company Postmates in 2021, has been making Uber Eats deliveries in Los Angeles, Miami, Dallas, and dozens of other cities for several years now, using robots that look like autonomous shopping carts. Serve says its delivery robots can be a safer alternative to cars and help reduce traffic congestion since they operate mainly on sidewalks. Since the robots have a top speed of around 6 mph, there’s little to no risk to pedestrians.
In an interview with The Verge, Serve CEO Ali Kashani explained that opening the platform keeps the company from relying too much on big delivery apps, while also keeping the robots busy between the lunch and dinner rushes.
“The reality of food delivery platforms is that usually they dominate their markets,” Kashani said. “Food is generally very picky. So you have lunch, you have dinner. But then there are times in between. So again, having that diversification helps.”
“Food is generally very picky. So you have lunch, you have dinner. But then there are times in between. So again, having that diversification helps.”
— Serve CEO Ali Kashani
By turning the fleet into what Kashani describes as an open marketplace, Serve’s robots will treat API requests the same as enterprise orders. “There’s no preferential treatment at the end of the day,” he said. “Until the robot is on a delivery, it doesn’t have a commitment to anybody.”
For small merchants, Kashani says the pay-per-delivery or hourly reservation options will undercut human-powered delivery services: “This would be a fraction of that cost.” Serve’s pitch also extends to intra-office shuttles, repair shops ferrying parts, and peer-to-peer exchanges like Facebook Marketplace. Developers supply the pickup and dropoff coordinates while Serve’s back end orchestrates obstacle avoidance, routing, and remote teleoperation supervision. Instead of hiring couriers or sending junior staff across town, businesses could program Serve’s robots to shuttle items between offices.
For Kashani, opening fleet access is the next phase in a long-standing crusade against last-mile delivery economics. “Why does getting something delivered from China cost $1, but from Chinatown cost $10?” Kashani said.
The problem is that delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats take a massive 15 percent to 30 percent cut on every order, largely because paying human drivers is expensive. By letting businesses connect directly to its robot fleet through software, Serve allows local shops — like bakeries, florists, and pharmacies — to add robot delivery straight to their own websites and checkout registers without paying those steep middleman fees.
It’s better economics for Serve, too. Kashani connects lower per-delivery costs directly to fleet utilization and scale, arguing that expanding demand beyond peak restaurant hours into off-peak hours and new use cases drives overall operating and hardware costs down for everyone.
The developer platform comes on the heels of Serve’s announcement that it doesn’t plan to renew its partnership with Uber Eats, echoing similar moves across the transportation industry to build independent platforms.
Yet sidewalk autonomy remains governed by the laws of physics. Serve says access to its robots will still be strictly gated by manual approval by Serve’s employees to prevent hazardous deployments or illicit cargo. Liability on stolen or broken goods will also be subject to how individual partnerships are priced and insured, Kashani noted.
And don’t expect 50-pound sidewalk robots to morph into full-size vehicles. Kashani remains adamant that Serve won’t morph into a street-based delivery service anytime soon. If software developers want to automate the sidewalk, Serve will gladly sell them the wheels.

After 7 months, Glasswing overwelms maintainers with underwhelming findings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
22:17:56 UTC
07:17:56 KST

Key Takeaways:
- Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild. Of Anthropic’s 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed.
- Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation.
- Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn.
- Anthropic’s claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings.
- Anthropic’s OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question.
We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality.
As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign.
That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities.
If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts:
- Tracking CVEs Attributed to Anthropic Researchers and Project Glasswing - April 15
- Observations on Anthropic's Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger - June 9
- 1H-2026 State of Exploitation Report - July 28
- The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In - September 8
So let's look at the results…
Tracking Anthropic-Discovered Vulnerabilities
I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs. The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger, which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches.
My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked.
After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs.
For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself.
The Danger Narrative Isn't Adding Up
You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980)
Anthropic's Ledger Continues to Underwhelm
When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look.
Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as “True Positives”.
The trend since my September update is even more telling:
In two months, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 findings and fixed just 15 more. Duplicates went from two to thousands, which is exactly what I warned about in September: the longer findings sit, the more likely someone else finds and fixes them first. I don't know how anyone can read these numbers as anything but damning.
You may also notice a correction in my visual. There appears to be a bug on Anthropic's ledger that inflates the number of findings marked as disclosed. Check for yourself using the "disclosed" filter.
Anthropic's Pivot to OSS Scanner
Having humans triage every finding clearly didn't scale, and Anthropic has said as much. In its OSS Scanner launch post on October 8th, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6,000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings." It had also already sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports to maintainers who asked for everything in bulk.
So with the Glasswing open source initiative hitting a wall, launching a self-service OSS Scanner that projects can opt into makes sense. Maintainers can now request a scan and triage the findings themselves. Anthropic is upfront that these reports are "fully model-generated, without human review or triage" and that "it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid."
In other words, the triage bottleneck didn't go away. It moved to the maintainers. If the true positive rate is really as high as Anthropic claims, that shouldn't be a problem.
curl Gives Anthropic's OSS Scanner a Reality Check
Three days ago, Daniel Stenberg, who maintains curl, announced that the project had received a batch of 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic. Anthropic rated only one as medium severity and the rest as low. Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them.
Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden.
This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability.
It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing.
curl took a bold move by deciding to publish low and medium vulnerabilities findings publicly as issues for full transparency and we encourage other open source maintainers to follow their lead.
Takeaways After Seven Months
AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.
About VulnCheck
VulnCheck is helping organizations not just to solve the vulnerability prioritization challenge - we’re working to help equip any product manager, CSIRT/PSIRT or SecOps team and Threat Hunting team to get faster and more accurate with infinite efficiency using VulnCheck solutions.
We knew that we needed better data, faster across the board, in our industry. So that’s what we deliver to the market. We’re going to continue to deliver key insights on vulnerability management, exploitation and major trends we can extrapolate from our dataset to continuously support practitioners.
Are you interested in learning more? If so, VulnCheck's Exploit & Vulnerability Intelligence has broad threat actor coverage. Register and demo our data today.

For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself.
The Danger Narrative Isn't Adding Up
You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980)
Anthropic's Ledger Continues to Underwhelm
When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look.
Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as “True Positives”.
The trend since my September update is even more telling:
In two months, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 findings and fixed just 15 more. Duplicates went from two to thousands, which is exactly what I warned about in September: the longer findings sit, the more likely someone else finds and fixes them first. I don't know how anyone can read these numbers as anything but damning.
You may also notice a correction in my visual. There appears to be a bug on Anthropic's ledger that inflates the number of findings marked as disclosed. Check for yourself using the "disclosed" filter.
Anthropic's Pivot to OSS Scanner
Having humans triage every finding clearly didn't scale, and Anthropic has said as much. In its OSS Scanner launch post on October 8th, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6,000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings." It had also already sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports to maintainers who asked for everything in bulk.
So with the Glasswing open source initiative hitting a wall, launching a self-service OSS Scanner that projects can opt into makes sense. Maintainers can now request a scan and triage the findings themselves. Anthropic is upfront that these reports are "fully model-generated, without human review or triage" and that "it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid."
In other words, the triage bottleneck didn't go away. It moved to the maintainers. If the true positive rate is really as high as Anthropic claims, that shouldn't be a problem.
curl Gives Anthropic's OSS Scanner a Reality Check
Three days ago, Daniel Stenberg, who maintains curl, announced that the project had received a batch of 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic. Anthropic rated only one as medium severity and the rest as low. Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them.
Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden.
This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability.
It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing.
curl took a bold move by deciding to publish low and medium vulnerabilities findings publicly as issues for full transparency and we encourage other open source maintainers to follow their lead.
Takeaways After Seven Months
AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.

We knew that we needed better data, faster across the board, in our industry. So that’s what we deliver to the market. $30M Raised to Redo the CPU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
22:14:03 UTC
07:14:03 KST

$30M Raised to Redo the CPU
As of today, Tendrils has completed a $30M round led by Benchmark to rebuild general-purpose computing.
Contemporary CPUs are made under the constraint of backwards compatibility with sequential, single-core chips. Accumulated layers of historical designs are locking engineers into decisions dating back to the 1970s. As a result, all existing CPUs are bottlenecked by complex cache coherency protocols and elaborate reorder buffers. CPU scaling is sabotaged from the start. At Tendrils, we believe that the future of general-purpose computing lies beyond legacy architectures for legacy software.
Tendrils is answering the question: what if we redo the CPU? Instead of starting from a sequential design, we’re building our processor to have thousands of cores operating in parallel. This requires moving beyond the notion of shared mutable memory and linear instruction sequences. To make this possible, we’re working in tandem on the open-source language Vine, which has been designed from the beginning to target a new wave of parallel-first architectures.
We’re delighted to announce that Tendrils has raised $30 million to support this vision. This round is led by Benchmark, with significant participation from Visionaries Club, the UK Sovereign AI Fund, FR8, Antimatter, Cloudberry VC, Conviction, Embassy Ventures, and SV Angels. We are grateful for additional support provided by all of our angel investors. Additionally, we wish to extend a warm welcome to our newest board member, Jack Altman.
With thanks to all who have supported us,
The Tendrils Team
At Tendrils, we insist that the chips of the future will be a result of close collaboration between hardware and software engineers. If this strikes you, consider joining us.

New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
22:00:00 UTC
07:00:00 KST

New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program (politico.com) 19
			
		 	
				New York is launching a state-backed AI safety research center at Binghamton University that will independently study and test AI systems, develop safety and security techniques, and train researchers in responsible AI. "While the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said. "The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word." Politico reports:  The center -- which is funded by a $30 million gift from Bloomberg co-founder Tom Secunda and a $25 million research investment from SUNY and New York state -- is set to launch before New York's major AI safety law, the RAISE Act, comes into effect on Jan. 1. That will require submissions of detailed safety frameworks from AI companies operating in New York State, which Hochul's office hopes will be scrutinized by researchers at the new center.
"AI is opening up questions that scientists could not tackle before," said Secunda, who also serves as the board chair of Empire AI, a $500 million public-private partnership. "With Empire AI and researchers across New York, the Center can test systems independently and give public officials evidence they can use."
Over 80 leading scientists and researchers on AI systems from across New York state will contribute to the effort, which will be run by the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, according to details shared by Hochul's office. The initiative will be led by Jeannette Wing, the executive vice president for research at Columbia University, and Greg Morrisett, the vice provost of Cornell Tech.
"We need new techniques that can be applied to this new kind of system with swarms of autonomous agents acting independently and without control. How can you first detect that they're going to do harm, and how can you prevent them from doing harm?" said Wing. "The beauty of what's being proposed is that this state is committing resources to really light this up."

rVPN – stealth VPN with end-to-end encryption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
21:42:50 UTC
06:42:50 KST

rVPN is an open-source protocol that carries your traffic safely across the internet, indistinguishable from ordinary HTTPS, so it works even where VPNs are blocked.
We believe privacy should be proven, not promised. Every line is open to read, audit, and run yourself.
curl -fsSL https://assets.rvpn.org/install.sh | sudo bash  A censor watching the wire sees ordinary web traffic on port 443. No tell-tale handshake, no blockable fingerprint. If they probe the server, it answers like a normal website.
A Double Ratchet rekeys every message, so a stolen key never unlocks the past or the future.
Probe the endpoint and it serves a real decoy site. Nothing to confirm, nothing to block.
The core is written in Rust, so entire classes of vulnerability cannot occur.
One TLS connection per flow means hundreds of parallel sessions under load: slow to establish, and a shape worth flagging. Pooled multiplexing carries every flow over a handful of long-lived connections, so the wire stays small and ordinary no matter how busy you are.
Every flow pays a full TCP + TLS + WebSocket + X3DH handshake. A busy client holds hundreds of parallel TLS sessions to one server.
Flows share a small pool of long-lived connections. Credit-based flow control keeps bulk transfers from starving interactive ones, and reconnects resume TLS 1.3 tickets in a single round trip.
Every claim on this page maps to code you can read. Clone the repo, check out a tag, and build the exact binary we ship. Reproducible by design.
Read the whitepaper →
rVPN is free and open under AGPLv3, and always will be. Development is fully funded by PDG Global Limited; sales of the iOS and Android apps, together with donations, contribute towards development costs. The code never closes.
One protocol, every device. Native apps for phone and desktop, a command-line client for your servers, and the source code to port it anywhere we have not yet.
Free, open source, and ready on every platform. The apps are on the stores and the source is on GitHub today.

Oura announced its quarterly earnings today and said it agreed to acquire Counsel Health for $625 million, after adding the company’s AI chatbot to its app earlier this year. Counsel Health calls itself an “AI-native primary care company,” using the app to deliver AI-generated responses and insights based on users’ health data reported from their wearables that can then proceed to a conversation with one of its in-house physicians.
Oura is acquiring medical AI chatbot startup Counsel Health
Doctor visits could start with a readout of your Oura ring data.
Oura says it expects the deal to close before the end of the year.
Oura CEO Tom Hale said in an interview with Bloomberg that the acquisition is part of a plan to connect wearables, clinical AI, and access to doctors based on insights from biometric data to answer questions or monitor ongoing conditions. Counsel Health’s AI chatbot can connect Oura users to a real doctor directly from the app and draw on users’ biometric data from their wearables in its answers to medical questions. The plan they describe in the press release is to focus on three areas, including preventative care, acute care for episodic health concerns, and specialty and chronic care for things like reproductive and cardiometabolic health.
According to Bloomberg, Counsel Health’s CEO Muthu Alagappan says it’s also planning to expand its network of on-demand physicians, which is currently “made up of about 50 people.” Counsel’s 70 employees will join Oura as part of the deal, with Alagappan becoming Oura’s chief clinical AI officer. Oura says in its announcement that Counsel will also continue offering its medical AI platform outside of Oura’s user base through new and existing enterprise partners, including “health plans, health systems, consumer health organizations, and employers.”

Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
21:25:03 UTC
06:25:03 KST

Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs.
New ‘Harbor’ app revealed at Apple: ‘turns your Mac into a private AI inference server’
The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more.
It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server.
Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details:
As the post notes, here’s what the app does:
Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone.
And here are the feature highlights:
- Setup in minutes, not hours: “Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you’re running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.”
- Download and run models directly: “Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.”
- Cluster for scale: “Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer’s capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.”
Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead.
Are you interested in using Harbor on your Mac? Let us know in the comments.

I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
21:22:43 UTC
06:22:43 KST

Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud.
I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
After LG was accused of spying through its TVs, I wanted to see how other TV companies were collecting and protecting our data.
To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers.
Company representatives providing responses
Amazon: Eric Sveum, PR manager
Apple: Emily Ewing, public relations manager
Google: Alex García-Kummert, spokesperson
LG Electronics: Chris De Maria, director of public relations
Roku: Sarah Novatt, spokesperson
Samsung: Frank Giancamilli, corporate communications senior manager
TCL: Rob Manfredo, head of communications and events
One month ago, I invited 11 companies, including Amazon, Apple, Google, Hisense, LG, Panasonic, Roku, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Walmart’s Vizio to share those answers. We now have answers from the top three TV manufacturers as well as every major streaming device company. Some companies declined to answer. Below, you can see and compare how each company answered (or failed to answer) each question and then decide how you feel. (One company, Hisense, ignored our emails entirely.)
As you’ll see them say, some of this data collection is opt-in, and you can often opt out. We know that many TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) to figure out potentially everything we’re watching, and use that information to tailor ads, gather audience metrics, and serve up content recommendations based on our viewing habits. But though it sometimes seems like it’s required during the cavalcade of agreements thrown at us during setup, you can generally stop ACR even after you’ve agreed to it.
Opting out might not be as effective as it should be, however. A recent Northeastern University study found that Walmart’s Vizio kept on sending data after an opt-out (Vizio told me it was “routine operational data used to support the Vizio experience,” not ACR), while traffic with both Samsung and Roku was limited, but not stopped completely.
Below are the answers to our 17 questions. You will notice that some companies would not answer yes or no. We’ve also noted where companies declined to answer at all or ignored the questions. If any company becomes willing to directly answer our questions, we’ll add their responses.
1. Do your TVs ever use their embedded microphones, or the microphones in their remotes, to listen to sound in a customer’s home?
Amazon:
No. Fire TV includes voice functionality to help customers use their devices and get to content they love and fast, not to surveil homes. The microphones on our voice remotes are designed to only work when the mic button on the remote is physically pressed. And TVs with hands-free Alexa are designed to detect the wake word (and only the wake word) before connecting to Alexa. No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word. Customers can also turn off the microphones at any time. Every Fire TV smart television that has microphones also has a physical button or switch that disables the microphone.
Apple:
Apple TV 4K will use its far-field microphones and the Always On Processor strictly to listen for the Siri wake word. The Always On Processor does not process or act on any other sounds in the home. Users have full control over this and can turn off “Siri” or “Hey Siri” as a wake word, or disable Siri entirely. When using the Siri Remote, users must actively press and hold the microphone button for it to start listening.
Google:
If Google Assistant or Gemini is enabled or available, microphones (built-in hands-free ‘Hey Google’ or remote push-to-talk button) listen for activation triggers. Microphones remain in passive standby until triggered by hotword or button press.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.
LG:
Voice recognition is off by default and operates only if the user has opted in by accepting the Voice Information Agreement. Even if the user has opted in, they need to take additional steps for the microphone to be used. They must either press the microphone button on the remote control or they can use Hands-free Voice Control on supported models.
Hands-free Voice Control is disabled unless a user opts into this feature and then uses a wake-word. Wake-word detection is performed locally on the TV. If no wake word is detected, the audio is processed locally, promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.
Roku:
While Roku TVs don’t have built-in microphones, some Roku remotes do. Standard voice remotes listen only while the mic button is held, and hands-free remotes can be switched off.
Samsung:
No, for private monitoring. Samsung TVs do not listen to or record private conversations.
The TV’s embedded microphone only listens locally for the specific wake-up word (like “Hi, Bixby”) and ignores all other sounds, while the remote control microphone only activates when the customer physically presses the button.
Sony:
Sony did not provide an answer to this question.
TCL:
Some TCL TVs and remotes have microphones. Users can activate those microphones to use voice assistance features provided through third-party operating systems or applications. Those third parties control whether the voice features are available and how they are used, under their own terms and privacy policies.
Vizio:
Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.
2. Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?
Amazon:
No.
Apple:
Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.
Google:
[Recorded audio and/or transcripts based on audio are] stored only if ‘Voice & Audio Activity’ (VAA) is explicitly enabled under Google Account Web & App Activity. Voice & Audio Activity is off by default. If VAA is off, voice requests are processed in real-time and not saved to the Google Account.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.
LG:
If voice recognition is enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control’s microphone button or using the wake word), certain information generated as part of a specific voice recognition interaction may be stored locally on the TV to support voice-related features. Depending on the interaction, this may include Speech-to-text results derived from a user’s voice command.
Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, captured audio is promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.
Roku:
Voice commands made via voice-enabled remotes may be retained to improve voice features and provide support, consistent with Roku’s privacy policy. Users can opt out in their Roku account privacy settings.
Samsung:
No. Samsung Smart TVs do not store voice recordings or transcripts on the device.
However, on secure servers, voice commands and transcripts are stored only to process requests and improve voice assistant services.
Sony:
Sony did not provide an answer to this question.
TCL:
TCL does not collect audio data from TCL TV or remote microphones, or from the use of third-party voice features.
Vizio:
Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.
3. Do your TVs transmit any audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?
Amazon:
When customers speak to Alexa by pressing the mic button on the remote or using their chosen wake word, a recording of the request is sent to Amazon’s cloud, where a text transcript of the request is created to help Alexa provide a response. No audio is captured without the customer invoking Alexa—either by pressing the mic button or saying the wake word—and customers can easily review exactly what they asked and what Alexa heard, delete their recording, or even choose not to save them at all.
Apple:
Siri AI processes user requests using on-device processing, and when a request needs more powerful AI models, it extends those same on-device privacy protections to the cloud through a groundbreaking infrastructure called Private Cloud Compute (PCC). When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple, or anyone else, and outside experts can verify this privacy promise at any time.
For moments when users ask a question that requires up‑to‑date information, Siri AI can go out to the web and find it, then use Private Cloud Compute to generate an answer. Searches and requests are associated with a random identifier — a long string of letters and numbers — not a user’s Apple Account.

OpenAI acquires Odessia, travel startup created by Sonder founder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
21:08:52 UTC
06:08:52 KST

OpenAI has acquired an AI travel agent called Odessia, according to Odessia’s founder, Francis Davidson. Davidson says in a post announcing the deal that he’s now working for OpenAI, helping the AI lab with the future of travel.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but this looks like an acqui-hire. Davidson’s announcement focused largely on how he built his AI travel agent Odessia by directing teams of AI agents. The year-old Odessia raised a $6 million pre-seed round led by Sequoia and launched its AI travel agent around five months ago. Davidson says that it had helped early adopters plan millions of dollars’ worth of travel, but the tool has already been shut down.
An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the hire to TechCrunch. “We’re thrilled to welcome Francis to OpenAI. Francis is a proven founder who has built multiple businesses to help people travel, and we’re excited he’s chosen to build with us.”
However the AI lab has not announced new travel-specific products or plans. It does, however, count such companies as Bookings.com, Expedia, and KAYAK as customers or partners. Travel is also one of the main areas that people are using personal AI assistants to help with. And, back in July 2025, when OpenAI launched its ChatGPT agent, it mentioned travel as one of its potential uses.
OpenAI’s spokesperson didn’t have more to share on its plans for travel-related products, except to say that travel is one of the areas that chatbot users frequently ask about. “1.2 billion people turn to ChatGPT each week for help with everyday tasks — from understanding their health, figuring out what to make for dinner, building a budget, and even planning a trip. We see a real opportunity to make these experiences even more useful,” the spokesperson said.
Acquiring Odessia is interesting for another reason. Davidson is well known in the travel industry after he founded a travel startup called Sonder as a college student in 2014. It was sort of like Airbnb, but it focused on short-term leasing of upscale apartments in major cities worldwide. The pandemic badly hurt it, and as it climbed out of that rut, it went public via a SPAC but didn’t raise as much money as it needed, Davidson later said in a post announcing his resignation as CEO in June 2025.
When a key partnership with Marriott fell through, the company went into bankruptcy and wound down. The bankruptcy trustee sold Sonder’s name, trademarks, and website domain in 2026 to TravelAI, and that website operates as a curated guide to the kind of travel rental properties that Sonder was once known for. Prior to its downfall, Davidson had built Sonder into a unicorn with over $600 million in revenues. While Sonder was not, ultimately, a success story, Davidson is the kind of battle-scarred founder that Silicon Valley often values.
So we’ll have to wait and see what OpenAI has in store with travel now that he’s joined the company.
Note: This story was updated with OpenAI’s comments and updated revenue for Sonder.
