Sony cancels live-service shooter Fairgames
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
21:06:12 UTC
06:06:12 KST

Sony has canceled Fairgames, a heist game announced in 2023, according to Bloomberg. Fairgames had once been part of Sony’s big planned push for PlayStation live service games, but the company ended up canceling some planned live service titles, including in the God of War and The Last of Us franchises, and it shut down Concord shortly after its failed launch.
Sony cancels live-service shooter Fairgames
Fairgames is PlayStation’s latest cancellation as it steps back from many of its live service efforts.
The Fairgames cancellation won’t result in job cuts, and developer Haven Studios will now support other PlayStation studios, Bloomberg reports. The game was canceled following a recent test where “player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set,” according to part of an executive memo published by Bloomberg, which also cited “challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre.” Sony acquired Haven Studios in 2022.
Sony’s live service efforts have seen some success with Helldivers 2, which is also available on Xbox. Bungie’s Marathon, which launched this year, has had a rough start, but today the studio showed off some new features coming in a December update, including a new co-op PvE roguelite mode and a PvP deathmatch mode. Sony is also working on a live service Horizon spinoff, but recently rebooted it.

The launch of Anthropic's new productivity-focused features comes just a few weeks after OpenAI unveiled a series of workplace tools that allow users to collaborate with ChatGPT to do things like visualize company information and create presentations, as both companies compete to turn their products into office suites of sorts to take on Microsoft and Google. Meta is also joining the competition with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly to help users complete specific tasks. Here's a summary of each of the offerings Anthropic announced today:
Claude Meetings: Allows Claude to join video calls as a visible participant, take notes, answer questions, retrieve information from connected apps, and create plans, timelines, and action items in real time. Available in beta for Team and Enterprise plans, initially supporting Google Meet.
Claude Whiteboards: A collaborative visual workspace where teams can brainstorm with Claude, organize ideas into timelines and plans, and turn their work into documents or slide decks. It also integrates with Claude Meetings to build whiteboards during conversations.
Claude Sheets: Lets teams create and collaboratively edit spreadsheets with Claude, including budgets and trackers with multiple tabs, formulas, formatting, and dropdown menus. Claude can make changes directly in cells while explaining its edits.
Anthropic also announced the general availability of Claude Data (formerly Claude Dashboards) that connects Claude to business systems like CRMs and data warehouses. "Users can ask questions, and Claude responds with dashboards, written data stories, or narrated videos," reports TechCrunch. Additionally, the company announced new interactive connectors that let users open Claude and work within third-party apps like Adobe, Atlassian, and HubSpot.

Terence Tao · original page
In Six Math Essentials, the renowned mathematician and Fields Medalist Terence Tao introduces readers to six central concepts that have guided mathematicians from antiquity to the frontiers of what we know today and now help us make sense of our complex world. This slim, elegant volume explores numbers as the gateway to quantitative thinking; algebra as the gateway to abstraction; geometry as a way to calculate beyond what we can see; probability as a tool to navigate uncertainty with rigorous thinking; analysis as a means to tame the very large or the very small; and dynamics as the mathematics of change.

Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
20:56:16 UTC
05:56:16 KST

Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890)
Approved July 2, 1890, The Sherman Anti-Trust Act was the first Federal act that outlawed monopolistic business practices.
The Sherman Anti-trust Act of 1890 was the first measure passed by the U.S. Congress to prohibit trusts. It was named for Senator John Sherman of Ohio, who was a chairman of the Senate finance committee and the Secretary of the Treasury under President Hayes.
Several states had passed similar laws, but they were limited to intrastate businesses. The Sherman Antitrust Act was based on the constitutional power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce. (For more background, see previous milestone documents: the Constitution, Gibbons v. Ogden, and the Interstate Commerce Act.)
The Sherman Anti-Trust Act passed the Senate by a vote of 51–1 on April 8, 1890, and the House by a unanimous vote of 242–0 on June 20, 1890. President Benjamin Harrison signed the bill into law on July 2, 1890.
A trust is an arrangement by which stockholders in several companies transfer their shares to a single set of trustees. In exchange, the stockholders receive a certificate entitling them to a specified share of the consolidated earnings of the jointly managed companies.
Toward the end of the 19th century, trusts come to dominate a number of major industries, destroying competition. For example, on January 2, 1882, the Standard Oil Trust was formed. Attorney Samuel Dodd of Standard Oil first had the idea of a trust. A board of trustees was set up, and all the Standard properties were placed in its hands. Every stockholder received 20 trust certificates for each share of Standard Oil stock. All the profits of the component companies were sent to the nine trustees, who determined the dividends. The nine trustees elected the directors and officers of all the component companies. This allowed Standard Oil to function as a monopoly since the nine trustees ran all the component companies.
The Sherman Anti-Trust Act authorized the federal government to institute proceedings against trusts in order to dissolve them. Any combination "in the form of trust or otherwise that was in restraint of trade or commerce among the several states, or with foreign nations" was declared illegal. Persons forming such combinations were subject to fines of $5,000 and a year in jail. Individuals and companies suffering losses because of trusts were permitted to sue in federal court for triple damages.
The act was designed to restore competition, but it was loosely worded and failed to define such critical terms as "trust," "combination," "conspiracy," and "monopoly." Five years later, the Supreme Court dismantled the act in United States v. E. C. Knight Company (1895). The Court ruled that the American Sugar Refining Company, one of the defendants in the case, had not violated the law even though the company controlled about 98% of all sugar refining in the United States. The Supreme Court reasoned that the company’s control of manufacture did not constitute a control of trade.
The E. C. Knight ruling seemed to end any government regulation of trusts. In spite of this, during President Theodore Roosevelt’s "trust busting" campaigns at the turn of the century, the Sherman Anti-Trust Act was used with considerable success. In 1904, the Supreme Court upheld the government’s suit to dissolve the Northern Securities Company in Northern Securities Co. v. United States. By 1911, President Taft had used the act against the Standard Oil Company and the American Tobacco Company. In the late 1990s, in another effort to ensure a competitive free market system, the federal government used the Sherman Anti-Trust Act, then over 100 years old, against the giant Microsoft computer software company.

OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York’s AI safety law takes effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
20:52:13 UTC
05:52:13 KST

New York is gearing up to enforce one of the country’s most significant AI safety laws. The state opened a registration portal Tuesday, with which large frontier AI developers like Anthropic and OpenAI will be required to register by January 1, 2027.
The RAISE Act, New York’s safety and transparency bill, kicks in at the start of the year. It mandates that large frontier developers — companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue — have to publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and issue public model transparency reports.
The newly formed Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) will implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI labs. Penalties can be as high as $1 million for one violation and $3 million for subsequent violations.
The state also can bring enforcement actions against companies that fail to register with the new portal, though a spokesperson declined to provide specifics.
“Tech moguls tell us that their vision for AI is inevitable,” Governor Kathy Hochul said Tuesday during a press briefing. “They tell us get on board or get left behind… That any collateral damage is worth it as long as we win the race to the AI cliff.”
On Tuesday, Hochul also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research based at State University of New York’s Binghamton University. The center will independently evaluate the safety, security, and operation of advanced AI systems and work with DIGIT to review companies’ safety frameworks. Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital.
“We’re building a national model for smart, sensible AI regulation, a model that puts communities above corporations and people above powerful technology,” Hochul said.
The RAISE Act isn’t the only safety law New York has passed. Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm.
In October, Hochul signed a separate chatbot safety law for minors, restricting behaviors like deceptive human-like interactions, emotionally manipulative or sycophantic responses, and encouragement of behaviors like suicide or disordered eating. That law takes effect June 1, 2027.
Other states have also passed similar AI safety and transparency bills to the RAISE Act. California’s SB 53, which took effect in January, mandates that frontier AI labs have in place and publish safety frameworks, enact whistleblower protections, and report critical safety incidents within 15 days. Illinois’ SB 315, which will go into effect at the start of 2027, has similar requirements, plus includes independent safety compliance audits.

Proximal Ventures raises debut fund to back startups bringing AI to drug development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
20:47:05 UTC
05:47:05 KST

While established venture firms continue to attract capital, first-time fund managers are facing one of the toughest fundraising environments in years. But that didn’t stop Sahir Raoof, a former SignalFire investor and executive at two healthcare startups, from raising $27.5 million for his first solo VC fund.
Raoof’s firm, Proximal Ventures, is betting that AI can transform the tools, infrastructure, and services that support drug development.
Pharmaceutical companies have historically outsourced various stages of drug development to specialized service providers, from synthesizing thousands of molecular compounds and figuring out how to manufacture drugs at scale to analyzing clinical trial data.
“For a long time, the assumption was that pharma is not a great buyer of software, but a really good buyer of services,” Raoof told TechCrunch.
Raoof believes AI could automate much of that work, creating an opportunity for startups to capture billions of dollars in pharmaceutical industry spending. By using AI, these companies could deliver the same services at a lower cost and in significantly less time, he said.
Some of the most valuable applications of AI so far have been in service-oriented industries like law and finance, Raoof said. He sees similar opportunities in pharmaceutical services.
Proximal plans to invest in pre-seed and seed-stage startups, writing checks from $500,000 to $1.5 million. The firm has already backed seven startups, including ChronicleBio, co-founded by former OpenAI executive Fidji Simo, which uses AI to analyze biological and medical data to better understand chronic diseases and identify potential treatments.
Before spending two years as a principal at SignalFire, Raoof led business development at clinical trial recruitment startup Iterative Health and previously oversaw partnerships at Flatiron Health, an oncology data company acquired by Roche for $1.9 billion in 2018.
“If you’re building a company that’s selling into the life sciences, one of the hardest things to do is starting that initial commercial flywheel,” Raoof said.
His sales chops, deep understanding of the healthcare ecosystem, and extensive industry relationships gave limited partners, the investors in VC funds, the confidence that he could spot strong startups and help them land customers. Proximal’s backers include VC firms SignalFire and Kleiner Perkins, Bertelsmann Healthcare Investments, and individual investors such as Dimension Capital co-founders Nan Li and Zavain Dar.
Amy Abernethy, co-founder of Highlander Health and former principal deputy commissioner of the FDA, is also an investor. She first met Raoof when they worked together at Flatiron Health, where she served as chief medical officer. She told TechCrunch that his ability to build relationships and spot industry bottlenecks made a lasting impression. Abernethy is convinced that his abilities, along with the understanding of what the healthcare market needs, will make him a successful investor.
It is these qualities that have helped Proximal invest in startups alongside some of the better-known, much larger funds, she added.

X-energy gets green light to build its first small modular nuclear reactors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
20:43:55 UTC
05:43:55 KST

Nuclear startup X-energy announced Monday that it had been given the go-ahead from federal officials to build its first four commercial reactors.
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved the construction permit application for four of X-energy’s Xe-100 reactors at a Dow chemical plant in Texas. Each reactor will be capable of generating 80 megawatts of electricity and 200 megawatts of heat. X-energy says the approval is the first for an advanced nuclear reactor at an industrial site in the United States.
The U.S. nuclear industry has pinned its hopes on small modular reactors — or SMRs — like those being developed by X-energy. By shrinking the reactor, proponents say it will speed construction and reduce costs, though those advantages have yet to be proven. No SMR is currently in operation in the U.S., and X-energy says Dow’s reactors won’t be operational until the early 2030s.
X-energy claims that its reactor design, which flows helium gas over uranium-containing fuel pellets, is safer than many existing reactors, but the Union of Concerned Scientists questioned the claim and the speed with which X-energy received the permit.
“The NRC only accomplished this feat by pushing consideration of critical safety questions to a later date—issues the NRC should’ve fully resolved before green lighting construction,” Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety for the organization, said in a statement.
The nuclear industry has benefited from strong interest from hyperscalers and data center developers, who are desperate for any and all sources of electricity. Amazon’s Climate Pledge Fund led X-energy’s $500 million Series C-1, and the big tech company has also committed to buying 5 gigawatts of capacity from the nuclear startup.
X-energy rode that wave of excitement earlier this year when its April initial public offering raised $1 billion. But since then, investors’ optimism has tempered.
The hesitancy isn’t surprising: Nuclear power plants are expensive to build and can take years to complete. Eventually, X-energy hopes to rein in both time and cost, but its first reactors are likely to be pricey.
The new permit approval gave X-energy a small jolt yesterday, though it was only enough to recover last week’s losses. The company’s shares are trading at less than half their initial offering price.

Starlink Mini 2 Adds a Swappable Battery, Wi-Fi 6 (interestingengineering.com) 40
			
		 	
				SpaceX has unveiled the Starlink Mini 2, equipping the company's smallest satellite internet terminal with a removable 71Wh battery and Wi-Fi 6. Preorders are opening to select U.S. customers for $999, which also includes a year of Roam Unlimited service. Shipments are expected to begin in mid-December. InterestingEngineering reports:  The removable battery represents the biggest functional upgrade over the original Starlink Mini. Previously, users needed an external power source to operate the satellite terminal. That meant carrying additional equipment for camping trips, remote work, or extended journeys. Mini 2 addresses that limitation with a detachable 71 Wh battery pack. It weighs approximately 1.08 pounds (490 grams) and delivers up to 4.5 hours of connectivity. Owners can replace it with another charged battery when necessary.
The battery also features LED indicators and its own USB-C charging port. SpaceX supports 60-watt USB-C Power Delivery charging for the pack. The retail kit includes a compatible 60-watt wall adapter and a three-meter USB-C cable. Users can also power the terminal through USB-C without relying on its battery. A physical power button replaces the original model's simpler plug-and-play arrangement.
[...] SpaceX has also upgraded the wireless hardware from Wi-Fi 5 to Wi-Fi 6. The integrated router supports coverage across approximately 1,800 square feet (167 square meters). An IP67 rating provides additional protection against dust and water. Other hardware details include a foldable kickstand and a standard 1/4-inch-20 tripod mounting thread. The terminal also offers a 55-degree field of view for satellite acquisition.

All 7 Anthropic founders will each cash out about $250M in IPO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
19:57:52 UTC
04:57:52 KST

As Anthropic barrels toward an enormous IPO that could value it at $1.4 trillion, the company has disclosed a tidbit in its new S-1 filing about how many shares each of its seven co-founders plan to sell.
Each will sell 3,378,378 shares. Anthropic has floated an unusually broad initial price range of $70 to $78 a share. At the midrange of $74, each founder would take in just shy of $250 million.
At the low end, $70, each would have to settle for pocketing just over $236 million in cash; at the high end, $78, each would take in just under $264 million.
However, in an IPO as eagerly anticipated as this one, companies can often price shares above the initial range.
The S-1 is already hinting at high demand. Board member Reed Hastings has indicated he wants to buy $300 million worth of shares through his donor-advised fund. Board member Christopher Liddell also wants to buy $3 million worth of shares.
The seven co-founders are Dario Amodei, CEO; Daniela Amodei, president and chair of the board; Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of public benefit; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer (pictured above); Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Christopher Olah, interpretability research lead.
After the sale, each of them will own about 3.2% of the total outstanding Class A shares, the S-1 says, or roughly 22% collectively. That’s not their share of the company overall. Class A is just one of Anthropic’s share classes, and other holders, including Amazon and Google, hold nonvoting Class N shares, so the founders’ stake in the company’s total equity will be considerably smaller. Even still, they, as a group, remain in control of the company. Each will also receive one share of Class F stock, which carries supervoting rights. Collectively, the founders will control 51.1% of the votes, but no single founder will hold significantly more shares or votes than the others.
As is now industry lore, the seven left OpenAI to start Anthropic in 2021 after disagreements with OpenAI’s leadership over how AI should be built. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who held senior research and policy roles at OpenAI, were joined by five fellow OpenAI colleagues in forming a company that has said, very publicly and from the start, that it’s more focused on AI safety than its rivals, including the founders’ former employer.

Toyota brand Scion is back and it's going to sell a kei truck in America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
19:50:46 UTC
04:50:46 KST

When Toyota first introduced the Scion marque in 2003, it had one primary goal – sell cars to the younger generation. Its cars were cheaper and available in fun colors with fun names like “High Voltage Yellow” and “xPRESSO.” When I was a kid in the early 2000s, I often dreamed of one day owning a tC in Black Cherry Pearl and enjoyed lovingly calling xBs “toaster cars.” Over half of new Scions sold were to people under 35, and the tC boasted the youngest average buyer age in the entire industry at a sprightly 29. Their sales numbers peaked in 2006, but dropped nearly 75% by 2010. After sustained financial struggle, Toyota retired the marque in 2016. But now, a decade later, everyone’s favorite toaster brand is seemingly back.
Today, Toyota announced the official revival of Scion, but instead of being a quirky and budget-conscious line, they are becoming Toyota’s cornerstone of curiosity. Now called “Scion by Toyota,” it is being launched as a “freedom lab” where drivers can, and are encouraged to challenge conventional ways of thinking about mobility through design, vehicle concepts, and features.
“Okei,” let’s go.
Their first production vehicle is the KEI-01, an ultra-compact utility truck, otherwise known as a kei truck. Toyota will be using its existing manufacturing infrastructure in Indiana to “produce” them for sale in the American market. “Produce” is in quotation marks because the KEI-01 is quite literally a rebadged Toyota Pixis, which is a rebadged Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo Cab. Based on its initial imagery it is seemingly also still right-hand drive, and there’s no word on if a LHD variant will be available in the future.
With its friendly little 660cc engine and CVT transmission, the KEI-01 was certified to meet American low-speed vehicle safety standards, meaning it has a limited top speed of less than 25mph and is only legal on roads with a posted speed limit of less than 35mph. This makes it not really usable as a daily driver, but keeps it in this beautiful sweet spot where it has a shocking number of commercial and agricultural uses.
The KEI-01 has a 600-pound payload (which means cargo and passengers) and a three-way fold-down cargo bed, making it a well-equipped workhorse for use on farms and in warehouses. It’s only about 5 feet wide and 11 feet long, which makes it great for use as a delivery or work vehicle in dense, urban areas like New York City. Believe it or not, it also has 4WD, which means it can traverse uneven terrain in more rural areas with ease. And don’t worry if it’s hot outside, because heat and air conditioning are standard.
It’s worth noting that, while Kei trucks are currently sold new in the U.S. as “mini trucks” through independent distributors, this one is sold directly by Toyota. Before you rush to your local Toyota dealer to place a deposit, I’m going to have to burst your bubble a bit. Initially, the KEI 01 is only going to be available in a low-volume, niche pilot program entirely focused on fleet usage beginning in late 2027. Depending on performance and owner feedback, availability of the KEI-01 may eventually be expanded, but no further information is available from Toyota at the time.
The Hybrid Side-By-Side
Two other mobility concepts accompany the KEI-01 in the Scion by Toyota lineup, the SxS Concept and the BXE Concept.
The SxS Concept was unveiled at the 2025 SEMA Show as a purpose-built side-by-side all-terrain vehicle (click here for our coverage). Developed by Toyota North America, the off-road concept is outfitted with a turbocharged four-cylinder from the Tacoma making in the realm of 300hp. You won’t have to worry about your turbo spool scaring away local fauna, as it is equipped with a “Silent Mode,” which allows the driver to switch from the boisterous internal combustion system to a much more civilised fully electric driving mode. Unlike the KEI-01, the SxS Concept is still just that – a concept, with no current plans to have a version available to the public.
Last, but not least, is the BKE Concept. The BKE concept is entirely focused on personal mobility in the outdoors, filling the gap between the utility of the KEI-01 and the pure performance of the SxS Concept. Its small form factor and rugged tires make it an ideal off-roader for traversing narrow paths while being portable enough to stow away when not in use or easily tote around in the back of a car.
Top graphic image: Toyota

The PlayStation Plus PC app is shutting down next month
Unknown

What objective is reasoning solving?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
19:25:14 UTC
04:25:14 KST

There’s an intuitive but simplified picture of reasoning: let a model think for longer, and it’ll be more likely to be correct. This aligns well with our human intuition: spend more time and effort on thinking and it’s more likely that we’ll arrive at a correct answer.
But this picture doesn’t seem to explain everything. During RL training, models learn to write longer chains of thought, and they get more accurate as they do. Yet if you take a trained model and force any one chain to run longer, it helps for a while, then stops helping.1 Sometimes the answer even gets worse, as if it’s overthinking.2 If a chain of thought were truly converging toward some optimum, more steps shouldn’t make it worse. So is it really the length of each chain that helps at inference time? Or is it something more subtle?
This post is my attempt to clarify this confusion (mostly for myself) by looking at reasoning as pathfinding through token space. We’ll see that RL maximizes the probability of finding a path from $x$ to $\Scal_x$, but individual paths are not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. As a bonus, this perspective clarifies some odd observations about reasoning models, like unfaithful chains of thought and reward hacking.
Reasoning as pathfinding#
Ask a reasoning model the same math problem ten times and you’ll get ten different chains of thought. Rather than thinking of reasoning as one mysterious process heading toward an answer, let’s think of it as pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses one of them with each sample.
Consider the problem: “what’s $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + 10$”? One solution is to add the numbers one at a time: 1, 3, 6, 10, and so on up to 55. Another way is to pair them from the outside in: $1 + 10$, $2 + 9$, $3 + 8$, $4 + 7$ and $5 + 6$ each make 11, and five pairs of 11 make 55. Both of these paths land on the correct answer, 55.
We can think about reasoning as following this general pattern. We are given a starting point, the prompt, which we’ll call $x$. We want to find a path $z$ that starts from $x$ and ends at a correct answer $y$. To tell whether a path lands in the right place, we assume we have a verifier $r(x, y)$ that returns 1 if $y$ is correct and 0 if it isn’t.
So given a starting point $x$, we want to find a path of tokens $z$ that lands in the set
$$\Scal_x = \{y : r(x, y) = 1\}.$$
The figure at the top of this post sketches this picture. Each gray line is a sampled path: it starts from the prompt on the left, meanders in token space by sampling $z$, with some of these paths landing in $\Scal_x$.
Since many paths land in $\Scal_x$, the success probability adds up over all of them. Let $\pi(z \mid x)$ be the probability that the model generates the path $z$ given the prompt $x$, and $y(z)$ for the final answer at the end of $z$. The probability of success is the probability of generating each path, times the probability that path lands in $\Scal_x$, summed over every path:
$$p_x = \prob{\text{a path lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = \sum_{z} \underbrace{\pi(z \mid x)}_{\text{samples path } z}\; \underbrace{\prob{y(z) \in \Scal_x \mid z}}_{\text{path } z \text{ lands in }\Scal_x}.$$
The second factor is just 1 if the path lands in $\Scal_x$ and 0 if it doesn’t, so we sum only the probability of paths that land in $\Scal_x$:
$$p_x = \sum_{z} \pi(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} = \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi(z \mid x).$$
We’ll call $p_x$ the success probability. Maximizing this probability means our model will be more likely to sample a path that lands in $\Scal_x$.
Note that there are two ways of increasing this probability. Either the model can sample multiple paths to the same answer, each with a small probability, or the model can sample a single path to the answer with a very high probability. The success probability doesn’t care which one we get, but in practice we might want to prioritize specific paths or ensure diversity in the samples3.
How do we boost our success probability?#
Best-of-$k$ sampling#
The simplest way to pathfind is to have the model $\pi$ keep sampling paths $z$ until one lands in $\Scal_x$.
Since we assumed we had a verifier, we can do best-of-$k$ sampling, which samples $k$ paths and looks for a success. Each path misses with probability $1 - p_x$, so all $k$ miss with probability $(1-p_x)^k$, and the success probability rises from $p_x$ to
$$\prob{\text{at least one of } k \text{ paths lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = 1 - \underbrace{(1-p_x)^k}_{\text{all } k \text{ paths miss}}.$$
This is a guaranteed axis of compute-scaling. As long as $p_x > 0$, the success probability increases monotonically as we sample more paths, so spending more compute on more samples always helps, as seen early on by Brown et al. 2024. However, the scaling here is over the number of samples rather than the length of the paths (thinking longer).
Train the model to generate better samples#
So far the model was fixed, so $p_x$ was fixed too. Can we change the model to increase $p_x$ itself?
Here’s a simple way to do this. Collect many prompts whose answers we can check. For each one, sample some paths from the model. We keep the paths that land in $\Scal_x$, and train the model on the ones we kept. Then repeat. Each round, we train the model to put more weight on the successful paths that it sampled. This loop is called rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and STaR was an early version of it for reasoning.
RL with a verifiable reward, which is how today’s reasoning models are trained, turns out to do almost the same thing. Let $\pi_\theta$ be the model with weights $\theta$. Then since $r(x, y(z)) = 1$ exactly when $y(z) \in \Scal_x$:
$$ \begin{aligned} p_x &= \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi_\theta(z \mid x) \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, r(x, y(z)) \\ &= \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))}, \end{aligned} $$
meaning the expected binary reward is exactly the success probability $p_x$.
Computing the gradient of the success probability via the log-derivative trick, we arrive at
$$\grad_\theta\, p_x = \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))\, \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z \mid x)},$$
which is exactly the policy gradient, also called the REINFORCE estimator. Now estimate this gradient with $N$ sampled paths $z_1, \dots, z_N$. The paths that failed have $r = 0$ and disappear, while the paths that land in $\Scal_x$ have $r = 1$. If $M$ of the $N$ paths succeed, the estimate is
$$\grad_\theta\, p_x \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x) = \underbrace{\frac{M}{N}}_{\text{success rate}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{M} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x)}_{\text{log likelihood of the successful paths}}.$$
This gradient involves two terms: the empirical success rate $M/N$ and the average log likelihood of the successful paths.
In other words, a step of REINFORCE with a binary reward is a step of rejection-sampling fine-tuning on the model’s own sampled paths, scaled by the current success rate $M/N$.
This also explains the first observation from the intro, that chains of thought get longer during RL training. Each step pulls the model toward the paths that landed, so if the paths that succeeded tended to be longer than the ones that failed (e.g. because they include backtracking behavior, gather more feedback from the environment, or just dumb luck), the model will learn to write longer paths.
Amortization and generalization#
During RL training, we spend a lot of compute to search for good paths and then we train the model to generate those paths directly. Once trained, the model can produce the answer without spending all this extra compute on sampling multiple paths. This is called amortizing the search: we pay for it once during training, so we don’t have to pay for it every time we ask the model a question.4 Since we train a single model on many prompts, the model can potentially generalize to new prompts it has never seen.
The figure below shows this for four prompts, each with its own $\Scal_x$, and switches between the model before and after training. During training, we sample paths from every prompt, keep the ones that succeed, and SFT on them. The percentages show the empirical rate of success given each prompt. The hollow prompt is new and not seen before by the model, but the model generalizes to this new prompt after training. As the new prompt gets further from the training distribution, its accuracy drops (try dragging it!).
Revisiting some observations about reasoning#
Once we see a reasoning model as a distribution trained to land in $\Scal_x$ given any $x$, a few odd facts about these models become clear.
Chains of thought are not guaranteed to be faithful#
Our verifier above only checks whether the answer is correct. The reward is 1 if $y(z) \in \Scal_x$ and 0 otherwise, so the intermediate tokens $z$ are just a way for the model to get to the answer. Nothing requires those tokens to be true, or to explain the answer that follows, though of course these are often correlated due to the model’s pretraining.
If we want meaningful chains of thought, we need to adjust the rewards or the training objective.
Reward hacking comes from both the verifier and the sampler#
We also assumed the verifier is never wrong, that $r(x, y)=1$ if and only if $y$ is actually the correct answer to $x$. But in practice the verifier can be imperfect. Then $\Scal_x$, the set of answers the verifier accepts, isn’t the same as the set of correct answers: it can include wrong answers and leave out correct ones. This misspecification opens up regions of $\Scal_x$ that the model might learn to land in even though it’s not what we intended.
Thus reward-hacking comes from an imperfect verifier, which fails to capture what we truly want, as well as an imperfect sampling procedure which fails to stay away from these shortcut regions.
In the figure below, the dashed circle is the set of correct answers and the red ellipse is $\Scal_x$. The ellipse stretches back toward the prompt, so its wrong answers are the easiest to reach, and after training most paths land there.
This visualization also shows why scaling up RL (generating more samples and longer samples) makes reward hacking more likely. The more extensively we “fuzz” the verifier, the more likely we’ll find a path that lands in the misspecified region of $\Scal_x$. Once the model finds this shortcut, training pushes the model towards similar behavior.
So what objective is reasoning solving?#
Reasoning isn’t actually solving any objective at all. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. It’s only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success.
RL training directly raises the success probability $p_x$, by spending a lot of compute on searching for successful paths and then training the model to reproduce them. Thinking longer helps because training taught the model to use the extra tokens, not because generating more tokens is intrinsically better. The cost of sampling during RL is amortized into the weights. At inference time the model is likely to succeed with a single sample, but any individual sample is not guaranteed to succeed.
- Muennighoff et al. 2025 forced a model to keep thinking by appending “Wait” whenever it tried to stop. Accuracy rose at first, and then flattened. ↩︎
- A neat example is Gema et al. 2025 which found tasks where longer reasoning resulted in worse accuracy. ↩︎
- We might revisit this in a future post. ↩︎
- This idea of using expensive search to find a better answer and then training a network to output the answer cheaply, shows up outside language models too. AlphaZero runs a tree search at every move of self-play and trains its policy network to prefer the moves that were found (expert iteration is the same idea). Physicists and weather forecasters do it with simulators: they run an expensive hand-crafted simulation to get an answer, then train a neural network to predict that answer directly. ↩︎

Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M

Oura announced on Tuesday that it’s acquiring AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million. The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”
Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians. Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June.
Users can connect with Counsel’s medical AI to get personalized medical advice, and chat with a physician when needed, all within the Oura app. Now, the companies plan to expand on their existing partnership to build across preventative care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care.
While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care.
“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release.
Counsel Health raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and GV. PitchBook estimates it had raised a total of $36 million.
Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership.
Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company’s 70 employees, Bloomberg reports.
“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Alagappan said in the press release. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care. From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”
The deal is expected to close before the end of 2027.
Oura also announced that its revenue grew 153% year-over-year to $533 million for the quarter ended on September 30. For its fiscal year 2026, Oura generated revenue of approximately $1.75 billion, marking 92% year-over-year growth.
The company reached an $11 billion valuation following a $900 million late-stage funding round in October 2025.

The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it

As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket.
The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested.
Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI.
“With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”
Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute.
For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged.
Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI.
Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”
It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China.
Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says.
Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions.
Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge. “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.”
The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says.
Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan.
“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.”
But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke.
“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says.
Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations. If those distractions begin to affect Nvidia’s ability to execute — slowing decisions, product rollouts, or the allocation of already scarce chips — the consequences could quickly reach customers. The AI labs and hyperscalers such as OpenAI and Anthropic “could have a real issue accessing the vast amounts of compute they need,” Kilcrease says, adding that switching to other hardware “takes time.”
In a race to build increasingly powerful AI, time is a precious resource. Experts say China trails the US closely, meaning that even modest delays for American companies can help Chinese rivals catch up. Nvidia is almost certain to face further disruption as investigations continue, though the extent to which the turmoil will roil the rest of the industry may be difficult to measure.
For China, however, the scandal could be about to backfire spectacularly now everything is out in the open. “The odds of AI chip control legislation being passed in Congress just went through the roof,” Kilcrease says.
Correction, Tuesday November 10th: A sentence in this article misstated that Anthropic is the leader in advanced computer chips. It is Nvidia.

A comprehensive study of how fingerprintable users are
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
19:03:54 UTC
04:03:54 KST

Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild
1Mozilla Corporation · 2University of Toronto · 3UC San Diego
This is the companion site to a study Mozilla ran on browser fingerprinting. With the help of almost 25 million Firefox release users, we measured how identifiable browsers really are, found which characteristics make them unique, and used that to design the fingerprinting protections that shipped in Firefox 143. Here you can read the paper and its key findings, browse the full appendix data the PDF had no room for, download the privacy-preserving aggregate data and analysis code, learn how the data was collected, and run an interactive test that compares your own browser against the measured population. If you have a question the data could answer, there is also a discussion board for proposing follow-up research.
Browser fingerprinting is a known tracking mechanism on the modern web, but its real-world effectiveness toward users has been hard to measure. To build robust protections, we measured uniqueness across a large, unbiased population, to determined what individual metrics cause users to be unique. These measurements used multiple privacy preserving technologies, like OHTTP, to ensure that no individual users can be identified or tracked across the web. The protections we built into Firefox avoid web compatibility problems while dropping the percentage of uniquely identifiable users from 75% to 46%.
Paper abstract
Web browser fingerprinting has become a key tracking mechanism on the modern web, yet its real-world effectiveness and which of the existing mitigations offer value at scale remain insufficiently understood.
In this paper, we present a large-scale study of browser fingerprinting based on real-world telemetry from almost 25 million Firefox release users. This dataset enables us to quantify user uniqueness at population scale and identify which characteristics contribute most to this uniqueness.
Our analysis shows fingerprintability is largely driven by a small set of high-impact characteristics and their combinations, rather than the accumulation of many independent measurements. Building on these insights, we propose and evaluate fingerprinting protections based on their impact on uniqueness and cohort structure, and design data-driven mitigations.
These protections, shipped in Firefox 143, reduce the fraction of uniquely identifiable users from 75% to 46% while maintaining web compatibility, demonstrating that practical reductions in fingerprintability are achievable in a mainstream browser.
Our key findings
Here's what we want to present to you with this paper and the broader scope of our work.
- Uniqueness is caused by a small number of metrics - not one or thirty
- Fingerprinting test sites have a seemingly endless list of measurements they can pull from your browser. If a user has a unique fingerprint, it is typically not because of a single measurement, but it is also not because of 20 or 30 measurements. It is a small number of metrics that make users unique. In fact, it's very close to the 80/20 rule. Specifically, of all the users seen as unique by Fingerprint Pro (the most discerning fingerprinter we model) - 80% of them are unique after only 8 metrics - while the fingerprinter collects a total of over 50 metrics. Signifyd collects more metrics, but identifies fewer users as unique: 80% of the users it sees as unique will be identified after 9 metrics despite collecting over 80.
- The numbers only mean anything per operating system
- Whenever someone cites a single percentage when describing "How many users are unique" - you should be suspicious. Because this collapses multiple different populations that behave very differently. Firstly, as a baseline, your operating system is always going to be exposed to a fingerprinter. We are always working within the constraint of web compatibility, and lying about the user's operating system breaks shortcut keys and gives you the wrong downloads among other problems. So if we know the website is going to learn your real OS anyway, we can use it to segment the population and analyze it separately. And when you do you see that each operating system behaves differently because they have different important metrics. Admittedly, it's very difficult to give a concise summary of work and also provide four sets of numbers - so even we fall prey to the trap of providing a single number, as we did in the prior paragraph. But every time we have a single percentage, somewhere we have that number broken down by operating system, and in doing so, you will see that each behaves differently.
- Entropy is not the measurement you want
- It's so, so easy to take all the results for a metric and just calculate Shannon entropy - it's a standard yardstick in this literature. But as we show - a high Shannon entropy does not reliably predict fingerprinting impact.
- Cohort size, not just uniqueness
- Previous analyses calculated how many people were unique, but they did not analyze the other people - the ones who weren't. All those other people might be 1 million users who share one fingerprint or 500,000 distinct fingerprints shared by 2 people each - that's quite the difference. We use the Simpson Index (aka the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index) to quantify that difference and compare different sets of cohorts (shared fingerprints). This lets us compare how effective different fingerprinting defenses are based not just on how much uniqueness they eliminate but how much they collapse groups of users into each other. For example, two different protections can each lower the share of unique users by about 2.1 percentage points. But one improves the cohort score by 56%, while another raises it by only 13%. Judged on uniqueness alone, two defenses can look equally effective; while the cohort improvement varies significantly.
- The same protection performs very differently per platform
- Protections are not uniformly impactful, and the variation is not small. As an example, clamping the available screen resolution takes 25.3 percentage points off cumulative macOS uniqueness but between 0 and 3 points off the other three platforms. Averaged across all users, that 25-point drop shrinks to 3.5 - a protection that matters enormously to one platform can look marginal in the aggregate. This is yet another reason why it's so important to segment and analyze data on a per-operating-system basis.
- Standardization and randomization go hand-in-hand
- Making users report the same values makes them look more alike, but it never makes everyone look the same. Some users will still stand out, and that gets worse on websites with small visitor populations. Standardization improves the situation, but it should still be paired with randomization. Randomization is very strong when it works, but can always be detected and bypassed. Neither can carry the burden of providing privacy on its own.
- The data shows why values differ, not just that they do
- Correlating fingerprinting values with users' hardware and other characteristics let us identify why certain measurements differed between users. Knowing the root cause lets us build protections that reach much further, and protect small groups of users who would otherwise stand out as a minority. Addressing these differences has already produced more consistent outputs for image rendering, Web Audio, and mathematical operations on Android, with more root causes being investigated.
- Users don't connect website breakage to the setting
- Breakage from a strict mode is delayed, and the delay hides the cause. Turning on a stricter mode is a one-time act - but the broken website arrives later and nothing connects the two. From the user's perspective, this website doesn't work in Firefox and they have no idea why and are frustrated. Report after report we see people posting for help, confused - despite having taken specific action to enable a hidden setting opting them into strict fingerprinting protections.
- Protections that ship have to keep the web working
- Users don't realize that a setting they changed caused the breakage, and don't know how to fix it - so a protection that breaks the web breaks the browser along with it. We selected and tuned mitigations on both measured impact and compatibility. For a default, compatibility isn't a trade-off against privacy - it's a precondition for it.
- The hard part is finding what breaks
- The web is vast, and even the most innocuous change is likely to break something somewhere. Some breakage can be anticipated, which helps design, testing, and detection. The other breakage gets fixed only if a chain of luck holds: someone has to recognize the breakage, report it, reproduce it on the right hardware, and get it to the right person.
- We are deliberately not publishing everything we could
- Commercial fingerprinters evolve continuously, and they borrow openly from the community that studies them. Sites built to teach people about fingerprinting - CreepJS among them - get picked up and used outright by fingerprinting products. So we have been deliberately conservative. There are analyses this dataset would support that we have not run, data we could have released that we have not, and offensive angles on this work that we have not pursued. That is a choice rather than an oversight: we would rather leave a question open than make it easier to build a better fingerprinter.
Test your own browser
This interactive test re-implements individual measurements as close as possible to how Firefox's own collection code performed them, runs in your browser, and compares each result against the published aggregate data. For every characteristic you can see your value and how many of the ~25 million measured browsers share it - overall and within your operating system.
The test runs entirely in your browser. All comparisons happen locally, against our static reference files. No data is stored or submitted to us.
If the test, or anything else on this site, looks wrong, please report it as an issue on GitHub. For a problem with the test, include the diagnostics from its Copy diagnostics button, or, if you would rather not post your measured values publicly, email them to tom@ritter.vg.
Paper
The extended version of the paper is available as a PDF.
Full appendix data
The paper's appendices contain a wealth of data locked behind a reasonable page limit and PDF formatting. This full data page carries all of it - every rank for every operating system and all three modeled services, the complete protection chains, and the paper's figures regenerated at print resolution.
Data collection
      Our measurements come from Firefox telemetry, specifically the 
      user-characteristics ping, a dedicated telemetry ping.
      Unlike normal telemetry pings that are sent regularly, this ping
      must be explicitly enabled (which has happened twice, once in 2025
      and once in 2026), and sends one data report before becoming dormant
      again.
    
This ping carries no client ID, only a UUID unique to the ping used to de-duplicate users. It cannot be keyed to any other telemetry submissions. It is submitted over Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP): a relay operated independently of Mozilla forwards the encrypted submission, so the relay can see the sender's IP address but not the contents, and Mozilla receives the contents but not the IP address. Access to the collected data was restricted to four authorized Mozilla employees. The data was retained for 90 days and has since been deleted.
Aggregate data & analysis code
We release four types of data:
- A list of fingerprints generated for different phases of protections, per modeled fingerprinter, with the user's OS and locale unmasked.
- Aggregate tables of the frequency of value per metric, split by OS
- Aggregate tables of the frequency of value per metric, correlated by other metrics' values, again split by OS
- A detailed analysis of rendered canvas images that allows comparison
In the fingerprint lists, the fingerprints cannot be recreated from a website measuring user characteristics, due to the way the telemetry was collected. After being generated, the files were shuffled to a new ordering, and any locale occurring fewer than 100 times was anonymized.
In the aggregate tables, any value observed fewer than 100 times within a single per-OS population is withheld - so the published data describes cohorts, never individuals.
In the canvas comparison, raw canvas renderings are provided, but they are devoid of any connection to other user data. Any unique canvas rendering is not provided; only the hash.
For verification and exploration, the code used to process the data and perform different analyses is available for review. It additionally contains the specific fingerprinting scripts captured, reverse engineered, and modeled for the paper.
Future Research
Far more can be asked of this dataset than we have asked. Some of it we chose not to pursue, some of it we simply did not think of, and some of it is a better fit for someone who is not us.
There is a discussion board for proposing follow-up analyses. Two kinds are worth posting:
- Answerable from the published aggregate data. Anyone can run these - the per-operating-system distributions are released, and the analysis toolkit is open. Post the question anyway, so the work is not duplicated and so the result lands somewhere others can find it.
- Needs the raw data. These we would have to run ourselves, since the underlying ping data is not something we can ever release. Describe what you want to know and why! To be clear, we do not have the raw data anymore but it is possible we will perform a re-collection in the future which we could analyze. We cannot promise to run everything, and some questions we will decline because we do not wish to help build a better fingerprinter.

PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
19:03:52 UTC
04:03:52 KST

David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.
“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”
The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.
The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.
More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.
“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”
That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.
“An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”
For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.
“Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”
Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.
“At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.
“If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”
As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.
“As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”
“We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”

The 12-month position is tasked with designing and implementing a "structured framework for organizing technical records, engineering documentation, source materials, and institutional knowledge related to legacy systems and platforms." Polygon reports:  In the past, Nintendo has drawn criticism from the preservation community. In 2022, the Video Game History Foundation publicly criticized the company for announcing it would be closing the Wii U and 3DS eShops. The foundation released a statement saying that Nintendo's decision was "actively destructive to video game history." The statement also pointed out that Nintendo is part of the Entertainment Software Association, which funds lobbying that prevents a number of preservation efforts.

OpenAI rolls out new business profiles, making ChatGPT just a little bit more like Google
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-10
18:49:52 UTC
03:49:52 KST

In an effort to make ChatGPT an even better consumer discovery engine, OpenAI is launching a host of new features designed to help companies control how users interact with their businesses.
On Tuesday, the company rolled out a Business Hub that will serve as a place where companies can create business profiles that — in a feature that greatly resembles the kind of profiles that Google and other search engines already offer — allow enterprises to verify and update information about their products and services. The feature is currently in beta.
Eligible companies will also be able to create and launch a specialized business agent, which gives ChatGPT users the ability to ask questions about the business and its products.
“As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI,” the company said on Tuesday. “Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT.”
In a move that calls to mind Google Analytics, the Business Hub will also give users access to limited business insights. These insights will reveal how ChatGPT users interact with their products — including profile views, business mentions, website clicks, and other metrics.
Businesses will have to verify their profiles through a formal process, although the company did not share specifics of what that process would entail. Benji Shomair, OpenAI’s VP of Monetization, told journalists on Monday that there are “multiple verification methods that we use for different types of business in different markets.”
OpenAI previously tried to position ChatGPT as an e-commerce hub by which users could buy products directly. This effort — which used a commission fee system — was viewed as a potentially huge source of revenue and a way to make ChatGPT a more direct Amazon competitor. However, that project ultimately failed to take off and, in March, the company retired the effort, which had even included a “checkout cart” feature.
With the integration of business profiles and intelligence, ChatGPT seems to be attempting to become more like Google, which — since the advent of the internet — has been the place where web users go to understand the companies they want to shop at. It remains to be seen whether this initiative will bear better results than the one that sought to make ChatGPT a direct e-commerce hub.

One of our favorite multi-filament 3D printers is $100 off

Bambu Lab P2S Combo
Bambu Lab’s P2S Combo is a 3D printer that can print in multiple colors and automatically dry its materials to help improve print quality. It also features a 5-inch touchscreen, a built-in camera for monitoring prints remotely, and AI-powered tools that can detect printing problems.
My colleague Sean Hollister praised the P2S printer for its consistency and hands-off approach to 3D printing.
